speechtext:
I think the point of
order is well taken, because as a matter of fact we are not discussing the position ,of the present member for Assiniboia, but an amendment which is now before the Committee. I understood the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) to refer to this matter merely by way of illustration. -

I bow to your ruling,
Mr. Chairman. My hon. friend (Mr. L. Thomson) has saved his friend from Assiniboia from further criticisms with regard to that agreement. If any other member had said as much as I have said, and I had an agreement of that kind in my pocket, I would produce it. I would stand by it or I would renege. I just want to register my protest against this un-British system of men coming here with the possibility of their being recalled by a handful of men in their own constituency or anywhere else. I was very much surprised that the hon. member (Mr. M. Clark) with his long parliamentary experience and thorough knowledge of British institutions should defend such a practice.

I can agree in two particulars, perhaps, with some hon. gentlemen who have spoken in , this discussion. I am not so mudh in love with the recall myself. Still, I believe .this amendment is not called for, that there is no good ground for it. As to another particular, I do not know that I can quite agree with any hon. members whom I have heard discussing it to-day-I have not heard all the discussion, but -most of it. It seems to be assumed that if a person signs such an agreement as has been mentioned, he cannot come here as a free and independent agent, that he cannot act independently. My hon. friend (Mr. Hocken) nods his .head. I am astonished, because I had a better opinion of him. I really thought he was more independent. I can sign all the agreements you like, and I would still feel that I could act here in an independent way. I do not require the recall, because the moment my constituents satisfy me that they want me to go back I 
will go without waiting for a recall. So what difference does it make if I have signed an agreement to go back providing the majority of my constituents are opposed to me, when I will go back if I am so satisfied without any such written agreement?

Did I understand the
hon. gentleman to say that he would sign an agreement to do a certain thing and that he would then not do it?

My hon. friend did
not understand me at all. I say that without signing an agreement I would go back in such a case. If I were satisfied that a majority of my constituents were opposed to me I would resign right now, without any written agreement. So the position is exactly the same. To show wherein I differ from some of the views expressed here to-day I cannot do better perhaps than to quote what I said in the House last year as reported in Hansard of the First Session of 1919, page 3579:
But so long as we are elected to represent the people of the country, so long as our constituents select us to voice their views, and we are called here for the purpose of considering and discussing public measures, it seems to me we are hound by our voices and votes to give effect, so far as we are able, to the desires of our constituents, at least in so far as we are able to understand these desires and can conscientiously support them ; and when we reach the stage where we feel that our own views and convictions are so far from being in accord with those of the majority of our constituents that we cannot properly represent them, we should resign and allow our constituents to select representatives who can represent them.
From tfhe discussion -this afternoon it would appear that members generally are entirely opposed to -those views, -although I thought at the time that they received the general approval of the House. I feel sure that if hon. gentlemen who have spoken would give voice -to their best thoughts they would agree with those sentiments; that we should, so far as we can conscientiously do so, represent -the views of our constituents, and when we -cannot conscientiously represent -the -majority, let us get out, because the people have a right to be represented here. I notice that a distinction is drawn between the ordinary common p opl'e and the cream of creation who -come here. I do not draw any such a distinction. It is said that the voice of the people is the voice of God. II think that is over-drawing it, but I think it is just as much the voice of God as is the voice of any clique here or elsewhere. I certainly dislike -what has been

preached in this House from time to time, that we are a sort of select (few who stand on a different level from the ordinary common people of the world. But we have that doctrine preached to us very often, perhaps not in so many words, hut in effect.
I believe that every member should not only represent the views of his constituents, but also do the best that in him lies for the benefit oif the country at large. My hon. friend (Mr. Hocken) looks doubtful, as if the two propositions were contradictory. They are not so in the least. 'Some people believe they are contradictory because they have not enough faith in theii constituents. I have sufficient faith in the constituents of Qu'Appelle to believe that they want me .to act here, not merely in their own interests, but in the best interests of the country as a whole. A great many hon. members apparently think .their constituents are so narrow-minded that they do not want their member to do anything except attend to their own special interests. I do not take that view of the people I represent, and the moment I do, I will get out, and very quickly, because I would not want to represent such narrow-minded people as a great many hon. members this afternoon seemed to think they were representing.
With regard to the recall, I am not in love with the principle. II do no.t say that I would not sign an agreement if I were asked to, 'because my position -would then be no different from what it is now. It is chips in porridge as to whether I sign such an agreement, just as it is with any other hon. member who is not so firmly attached to his seat that he is not prepared to leave it when he feels that he is not able to represent his constituents properly. My hon. friend (Mr. Hocken) asked how we would like hon. members before they come here to sign an agreement whereby fifteen manufacturers would have the power to recall them. I would not have the slightest objection, providing there were the safeguards that my hon. friends (Mr. 'Gould and Mr. Halbert) have mentioned, namely, that the majority-for that is what it practically amounts to-want the member recalled. As long as those fifteen men are honest, and can satisfy themselves that the majority of the constituents want the member recalled, there is no objection whatever to his being recalled. I think it would not be a bad idea if some of us were recalled.
That's bad doctrine.
I believe in the people ruling. My hon. friend does not.

I believe in all the people
ruling.

So do I. While I agree with my hon. friend that we should keep in mind the good of the people as a whole, my view is that the people of any particular locality who select a candidate and send him to Parliament have a right to have their special views represented in the House. I believe that we should bear always in mind the good of the whole people, and I believe that our constituents entertain that view. Before I was nominated at the last election I tried to make my position perfectly clear. My experience in the House had shown me-and it iwas not a very pleasant experience, I must say-that unfortunate situations might arise at times from a party point of view, that under certain circumstances a man had the right to use his own judgment and that it was not safe for him to depend on the views of any one else. I therefore said to my constituents: If you are going to select me as your candidate I want you to understand that I will go on one condition only, and that is, that I shall be entitled to use my own judgment in any case where I think necessary. And I said further: If you are not going to send me to Parliament on that condition I do not want the nomination', and I will not go.
That is not the case with your hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Gould).

Having made that perfectly clear, I was returned to Parliament iby acclamation, which I think showed that the people generally in my constituency held the same view that I hold, namely, that while to a large extent a member represents the views of his constituents, he must be given a free hand and be allowed to exercise his own judgment when circumstances demand that he should do so. <

Suppose, when the hon. member had put to his constituents in that manly way the position he took, they had said: That is all very well; now, will you sign your name to this agreement before you go to Ottawa?-what would he have said?

I would have no hesitation in signing it. I might not ap-
2C40

prove of the proposal in its entirety, hut I say that those people would have the right, if they saw fit, to ask that their views should he presented before Parliament. And without signing any agreement I represent their views now.
You would not regard that request of theirs as a mark of confidence, would you?

The fact that they have returned me to Parliament is a mark of their confidence in me. With regard to the remarks of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) and others in connection with the question of initiative and referendum, I do not see why certain constituencies should not do certain things they want to do if they see fit. I have no objection to the principle of initiative and referendum. I took my Stand on that question long ago, and am in favour of it; and if the majority of the people were in favour of recall I would accept it because I would be in a minority. My main objection to the recall is not the objection that has been urged here. I object on the ground that it would relieve the people themselves of a certain responsibility which they ought to shoulder. When the people of a constituency select a man to represent them for four or five years we have the right to expect that they shall exercise every care and precaution to ensure that the man whom they choose is a man in wham they can repose absolute confidence and on whom they can depend during the term he represents them in the House. I think we have the right to expect that the people should shoulder that responsibility, and that is the ground upon which I object to the recall. I do not object to the recall because I do not want to be recalled myself should a majority of the people (whom I represent be dissatisfied with the manner in which I have discharged my responsibilities to them. If I am fool enough not to know when the people are dissatisfied with the way in which I represent them I hope they will show me imy error. My hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) is a lawyer and should understand the legal effect of his amendment, and I think he will agree with me that that effect is that the agreement which is signed must be of such a character as to limit the independence of the member. If he considers for a moment I think he will agree that it will depend on the man himself as to whether his nomination is regular and legal. If the man were of such a character that his independ-
dence would not be affected it would be perfectly safe to nominate him; but who is to decide wfiether a man is of that calibre or not? Is it the returning officer who is to decide that point? The returning officer decides a great many things, but is he to call witnesses to decide whether the man nominated can be trusted to exercise his own independence in spite of his liability to be recalled? He must decide whether the man is so crooked and unreliable as not to be trusted to act on his best judgment for fear of being recalled. I think my hon. friend rwill see that there is a valid objection to his amendment as framed. If the man is worthy of nomination this amendment cannot apply to him, because a man is not worthy of nomination unless he is independent enough to act on his own (best judgment even though he expects to be recalled five minutes after.

I must eay that I am very much at sea after listening to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. L. Thomson). I do not know whether he proposes to vote on principle or in defiance of principle, or whether he agrees With the amendment or not. At one moment he says he agrees with it and at another he says- he does not. It is a case Of "now you see and now you don't." The fact that I cannot apprehend the exact view of my hon. friend is perhaps due to my unfortunate stupidity, but nevertheless that fact remains. If members of the House are sent by their constituents- with instructions to vote for the recall, the House will pass |a (law enacting the recall. I do not think there is .any doubt about that. So that saying that there shall be no recall or that the principle is wrong is surely beside the question. If the people elect members and send them to vote for recall, initiative and referendum, the whole three if you will, they certainly will vote for it. If they are not sent here for some specific purpose of that kind possibly it would be premature for them to do so. I can understand the agreement that some of these gentlemen are said to have signed. It is in anticipation of the legislation that is demanded by some, namely, that there should be the recall. As a consequence, the constituents, feeling that it ought to be the law, if it is not, require their member to sign some such agreement. I do not think that can be said in any way to restrict the independence of the member, because the member who is invited to represent the constituency is well aware of the restriction which exists, and moreover the mem-

ber is invited to represent the constituency, not himself. Many people run away with the idea that they are here to exercise their own judgment. They are certainly not, except within the limits of absolute right or wrong-which neither they nor anybody else can comprehend;-they are here to represent their constituents within reasonable limits and excepting some of the glaring measures now before the public which deny reason and right.
With-in reasonable limits therefore we may say that a man finds that some policy has arisen-such, for example, as the Canada Steamship merger or the steel merger, or the great agricultural merger that is now maturing, or something like that,-on which he has had no instuctions, but on which he may have very definite opinions. These opinions may be entirely contrary to the opinions of a great number of his constituents. Surely it would be absurd, within reasonable limits, that this man should not accept notification that he should return and confer with his constituents on the subject. In any event it will undoubtedly be the law some day that a member will take his membership on the understanding that all these restrictions apply; -if he does not like to take the job he can stay at home. But that this new law is coming is undoubted. I think anybody can see that everything that facilitates the movement of the machinery of legislation is likely to be enacted, and endorsed and received by the public.
Undoubtedly, sometimes, Mr. Chairman, it might not work well, but it is within the power of the constituents to see that it does. It is true that we have had measures adopted in this House which defy the constituents and that we have had members who have defied their constituents. The constituents are tired of that, and I fancy a good many of the members are, too. Democracy, instead of developing on democratic lines, has in the most extraordinary manner, as someone well expressed it the other day, settled itself in government. Privy councils were originated in the reign of the Stuarts for the purpose of curbing the power of the king. They were then supposed to represent the opinions of the people. But having disposed of the absolute authority of the king they have proceeded in these later days to dispose of the absolute authority of the people. These things must be said, and surely it is but common sense to say that the people who pay the taxes and bear the burden and heat of the day are entitled to be consulted.
While I myself personally would feel it a severe affliction, and a reflection upon my judgment, should the people take action by way of recall, I must nevertheless admit that it is right and reasonable, with proper safeguards, such as possibly twenty-five per cent or something of that description. I would be recreant to my duty if I did not speak in favour of that advanced principle. It may be possible that if we did confer with our constituents the member would convince them that they were wrong and he was right, in which case the blushing member, after he had converted his entire constituency, would return to Parliament in a great wave of popular approval and the offence which might be given to his isupersensitiveness would be compensated for by the acclaim with which he would be received in recognition of the astounding victory that he had achieved over his constituents. But do not let us commit the error of saying that we stand in the way of trying any reasonable measure which would allow us to confer with our constituents in order that they might express their opinion and that we might express ours.

Mr. Chairman, I have always supposed that the Conservative party of Alberta stole this plank of the recall from the platform of the Non-Partisan League which was strong in Alberta at that time. I am told also on good authority that this was a very astute expedient of the Conservative party in Alberta to put one over on the Non-Partisan League. The hon. member for West Calgary-

Will the hon. gentleman allow me to correct him?
Mr. J. F. REID-was the leader of that party at that time. I am not quite sure whether he was the recognized or official leader, but I do know that he was the man ''with the punch" behind the leader, if he was not the actual leader himself. On account of that I understand that the NonPartisan League in the province of Alberta has pretty well gone out of business, the assumption being that the Conservative party in Alberta became the Non-Partisan League whose strongest appeal was direct legislation.
Considerable has been said about signing an agreement. An attack has been made on the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) because he signed an agreement which seems to tickle the curiosity of hon. members opposite. Why? The Conservative party was the party which in-

stituted this procedure. If the hon. member for Assiniboia has been guilty of the offence of signing an agreement, he is not the only one in this House who is guilty of it. There is an old Scotch' saying that you had better clean your own doorstep before you go abroad to clean the doorsteps of others. What is the difference between the procedure instituted by the Conservative party and signing an agreement such as the one which the hon. member for Assiniboia is understood to have signed? I am of the opinion that not one hon. member *on the other side of the House sits there a free man. I will endeavour to prove it. Is it not a fact that in the election of 1917, before hon. members received the endorsa-tion of Union Government, they promised allegiance to the Union Government?
Absolutely not.

 I came into the House to represent anything else but one of the best constituencies in the Dominion of Canada. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In view of the fact that this amendment has a direct bearing on the important question of the independence of members of Parliament I should not like it to go to a vote without expressing my views as to the significance of its proposal. In my opinion every member of Parliament should feel, if he wishes to represent the people in the broadest possible way, that when he enters this Parliament he is a representative not of any class, not of any creed, not of any section-I might say not of any particular constituency except to see that the views of his constituency are always properly presented-but that above all he represents the people of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific. That, I think, is the only view a man can take as to his responsible position as a member of the Parliament of Canada. Having stated my belief in that regard, may I consider the significance of the amendment and what it proposes?
All our political institutions are a matter more or less of evolution. There was a time when the Governor of this country thought that he could dictate to his ministers, and that the ministers should have no say whatever unless it suited the particular view which the Governor entertained. It was an attitude which - those who wanted things done only in accordance with -their	own way of thinking,
were apt to encourage. A familar example which will be in the minds of members of the House was the occasion when Lord Elgin was asked to assent to -the Rebellion Losses Bill which Parliament had passed in 1848. The Tories of that day thought that our governmental institutions were being outraged. They told Lord Elgin that if he assented to that Bill he would have to take all kinds of consequences, including his recall to England. What was the position that Lord Elgin took? He said that his advisers had given him the Bill to sign, and that he proposed

to accept the advice of his advisers. What was he told? I am not quoting the exact words, but they were to the effect that his advisers were fools. To this Lord Elgin is said to have replied: If the people care to send me fools as advisers, then I must abide by the advice of fools. In that expression we find the principle underlying responsible government. From that time to this it has been held that the Governor is bound by the advice of his ministers so long as they represent the people, and that it is not for the Governor to say who his advisers shall be.
It seems to me that in regard to this particular amendment we are in a position very similar, as respects what is fundamental in what we mean by representative government. It is for the people to say whom they wish to send to this Parliament as their representatives, not' for this Parliament to tell the people whom they shall or shall not send. If the people desire to choose as .a candidate and to send to this Parliament as their representative a man who is tied, manacled or bound, whether by physical infirmity, by agreement, or in any other way, so long as all the facts and circumstances surrounding his position are publicly known, it seems to me that, on the theory that the people have the right to govern and to send whom they will to Parliament, they have a right to say whether or not that candidate should go to Parliament.
Now, with regard to the particular matter of the recall, were I in an election and had I as an opponent-I understand that there is the possibility of such being the case-one who is bound by any recall, I should urge strongly upon the electors that that was one of the main reasons why they should not give him their support; that one who is bound by an agreement, fettered in any way, subjected to any restriction of his liberty in this Parliament to take whatever action seems best as questions come up, is not in the best position to serve as a representative of the people. That, I think, is a strong reason why such a candidate should not be returned.
But that is a very different thing from this Parliament here and now saying that they will not allow the people of the country the liberty to choose between a man who is bound by the recall and a man who is opposing him and who will not be bound in that way. Mr. Chairman, I feel that the question is one which affects the fundamental rights of the people in the matter of Government, and believing as I do that the people should have the full-
[Mr Mackenzie King.]
est liberty, the fullest freedom, in the choice of whom they wish to send to this Parliament, I shall oppose this amendment because I believe that it would deprive the people of a certain liberty in that regard. At the same time, I repeat what I said at the outset: that any member or any man who presents himself to the electorate and at the same time tells the electorate that he is not free in all particulars to use his best judgment as circumstances dictate, is not, to my way of thinking, the best type of representative to have in Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
To a very large extent, speaking for myself, I agree with the views just now expressed by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). However, I think it is just as well that this question has been ventilated in the House; I do not think that the time that has been taken up in this discussion will be found to be wholly unprofitable.
Perhaps, there is some misconception as to the real meaning of the amendment. If I read the amendment aright, it does not raise the question of the legislative recall as it has been discussed in this House today; it raises rather the question of agreements which would in any manner whatsoever limit the independence of members of Parliament. Having regard to the real meaning of the amendment, 1 think most hon. members will agree that any agreement which does limit the independence of a member of this House should not be permitted to exist. I have heard it stated by my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark), a man of broad learning and great experience, that these agreements are nothing more than political plfedges. If that were all, I would agree with him that there is very little wrong in them. But they are not political pledges. Political pledges are made in the open.
Not always.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Political pledges are
pledges made for the purpose of convincing an elector; they must foe .made in the open; they must be made notorious, or they will have no effect. The vitiating principle of such agreements as are referred to in this amendment, if I understand it aright, is the secrecy of the proceedings-a secrecy which, in the case of one agreement that I know of, an hon. member is determined to maintain. I heard my hon. Ifriend from Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) this afternoon say that he had been followed around this House by members who sought to obtain from him

the platform of tihe Farmers' party. Well, around the corridors of this House I have heard a good many members say that they would like to obtain, not the platform of the Farmers' party, but the secret agreement wihidh the Farmers' party insist that their candidates shall sign. Here is one principle to which I seriously object; that ten or fifteen or twenty men in any riding should hold any document of a secret nature-I emphasize that point, because if it is free and open I have no objection to it- which will in any way limit the independence otf a member of this House. It is a wrong principle; it is a vicious principle; in my humble judgment it is a principle which Parliament should seek to do away with. I do not know that the amendment now proposed is the correct remedy; probably it was launched for the purpose of having this question discussed. I believe that the whole of the people should be made acquainted with these facts. My position is this-and I think I can speak for the Government in this respect-that so long as your agreement is made public, so long as the people understand it before they take advantage of the opportunity of voting on it, II see no objection whatever to it. If a candidate for election as a member of this Parliament is bound by an agreement of a special nature to any particular class otf people, and If these facts are known, all well and good; let him go to the polls on that understanding. But the case is entirely different when the agreement is of a secret or private nature, if that agreement limits the independence otf the member of Parliament.
Will the hon. member allow me to tell him exactly what the Farmers' platform contains upon this question?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think I can dispense with that.
There is no secret agreement mentioned in it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I can dispense with that for the moment. It has been brought to my attention-rumours at all events are afloat to the effect-that in the Ontario legislature to-day men are sitting who have been elected and who have actually signed a form of resignation in the form prescribed by the Ontario Statute, which form is witnessed by two electors. These documents were signed,. I am told, before the nominations took place. Certainly, they were not made public before the election. If such
documents exist, if they are secret documents and if they are permitted by the law, then I say that the law should be amended. That is my personal view of the matter. I hardly think this amendment is in the proper form to remedy the matter; but the amendment has at least served one good purpose; it has brought the whole question to the attention of the House and of the country, and I think it is a subject which should receive the attention of the Government. I do not know what the ultimate object of my hon. friend (Mr. Tweedie) in moving this amendment is. I would suggest to him, now that we have had the benefit of this discussion, now that we have a better understanding of the whole subject, that a little time be permitted to us to study out the question and come to some conclusion on it after we have made a better and fuller study of it than we have made up to the present. My suggestion to the hon. member is that he should remain content with the discussion we have had and withdraw the present amendment.

I would be very glad to follow immediately the suggestion made by the Acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) who has charge of this Bill, and I can assure him that I shall follow his advice and the suggestions also of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), after I have made a few remarks which I feel I should make in justice to myself and those who have spoken on this side of the House in connection with this amendment. When I introduced this subject, I introduced it purely as a question of principle without having in mind the status of any individual member of this House. I endeavoured, so far as was within my power, to avoid any personalities in connection with the discussion. I did not wish, that any remarks that I made or any remarks which were made by any hon. member in support of the amendment which I moved should in any way be derogatory or belatting of or hold in ridicule any hon. member who felt it his duty to speak in connection with this amendment. To that, I will refer later.
I have no apologies to make for moving this amendment, because I feel that, in connection with the political life of this country, while the question has not yet assumed vast proportions, it is a growing question which must he dealt with, and if we are to conserve our constitutional rights, it behooves us, as members of this House

of Commons, to take into consideration and have in this House a frank discussion of the arguments which might be adduced for or against this question of the recall, the signing of a resignation before an election, or the entering into any agreement with any committee, which agreement might limit or control the activities or duties of a member of this House.
I cannot agree with the arguments which have been submitted by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) when, standing up in his place in this House as leader of one of the great parties of this country, he says that there is growing up in connection with our constitution a principle to which he cannot adhere and which he cannot support, and then says that he thinks it should be allowed to go unchecked. If this be a principle which is contrary to the constitution of this country, then it is our duty either to amend the constitution or to enact legislation which will prevent the circumvention of our constitution and the introduction of a system of-which we are not,, as a people cognizant.
A particular feature of this discussion which must certainly be very gratifying to every member of the House, is the free expression of opinion which we have here. The sentiments of members of the Opposition, as expressed by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's and the leader of the Opposition, go to show that that party with which they are allied do not believe in either the doctrine of the recall, or the doctrine of signing an advance resignation, or the doctrine of having any man who is a candidate in any constituency of this country enter into any agreement which is going to limit or fetter the exercise of his rights as a representative of the people in Parliament. But while it might be expected that the members of the Opposition would take that stand as. one of the old-line parties in this country,, and while we might look for expressions of opinion of that nature from this side of the House, a party which is composed of Liberals and Conservatives.
No, all Tories.

Well, I will say they
are all Tories, and I am glad my hon. friends recognize the conversion to the true principles which should govern this country. While I rejoice in that fact, I must say that I was greatly amazed and also greatly delighted when I heard the utterances of the representatives of the National Progressive Party in this country, as they 
have assumed to call themselves, or the agricultural or rural representatives. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. L. Thomson), who is a representative farmer, who supports the policy laid down by the Council of Agriculture of this Dominion, a policy which says that they believe in the initiative, the referendum and the recall-
No.

-that hon. gentleman
standing up in his place in the House says that he is not in favour of the recall. Let us consider the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. 'Clark), the hon. member who speaks with such eloquence, force and decision, the hon. member whose utterances on any question in this House are, so far as he is concerned, the last word to be said. That hon. gentleman, who speaks about myself having a lightning change of attitude, sits in this House as a member of the Farmers' Party in this country, a party which has as its platform the initiative, the referendum and the recall.
No.

In all my experience
in a legislature or in this Parliament, I have never yet witnessed such an exhibition of straddling as the hon. member for Red Deer has given to-day in connection with the stand which he takes on the recall, the advance resignation, or the entering into an agreement with any committee of men in regard to his decisions in the House of Commons. He refers to the amendment which I have moved, and in closing his remarks, he very patronizingly says that that amendment does not appeal to his intelligence. (But I am not responsible, Mr. 'Chairman, for the intelligence of the. hon. member for Red Deer. If I judge from the discussions which have taken place since the moving of my amendment this afternoon, I am sure the amendment appeals to the intelligence of almost every member in this House, and there are in it points which are worthy of consideration and discussion.
When he got up to reply 'he very patronisingly said that he could not congratulate the Opposition, he could not congratulate the supporters of the Government, and least of all could he congratulate the hon. member for West Calgary, the mover of the amendment in regard to their stand. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I do not hold my .seat in this House for the congratulations of the hon. member for Red Deer or anybody else, and if I were looking for congratulations in this House the hon.

member for Red Deer can rest assured that he is not the first man to whom I would appeal for congratulations. He takes the amendment, analyses it, and discusses it. He asks, what does it mean? He says: A man may want to enter into an agreement with his partner, but if this amendment passes he cannot enter into any such agreement Mr. Chairman, a man who has any intelligence, to use the hon. member's words, if he simply reads the amendment will see that it has no reference whatever to business-, but simply to- an agreement which limits the independence- of such person in the performance of his duties as a member in the event of his being elected to -the House of Commons. It has to do only with the performance of the duties of a member of this House, and it is immaterial whether a man enters- into any agreement with his partner in regard to their business relations, as to his willingness to resign or not to resign or business reasons relating only to himself and not to his constituents. It is immaterial whether he enters into an agreement with his wife before he leaves ho-me as to whether he will resign for family reasons. The question is, is he going to be allowed to -enter into any agreement, with -anybody which is going to interfere with his independence as a member of the House -of Commons or of the body in w-hich he sits? He also suggests that so -far as the mover -and the seconder of this amendment are concerned, they evidently did not consider fully the meaning of the amendment. Being an- old parliamentarian, -such as he is, a -man with much greater experience in political life than I have had, -he must realize that when you -are sitting . in Committee of the Whole House -there is simply the mover of the amendment. I have no seconder -and there never was a seconder to this amendment. The hon. member is therefore either ignorant or else he wishes to misinform the House and give a false impression to the people generally. There was no agreement between myself and any member who has spoken on the amendment. Many of those who- have made speeches- on the- amendment never saw it until it was presented. n

I *am about to close Mr. Chairman-
Some hon. MEMBEBS: Go on.

-but I want to point out that it would not be wise for the members of this House to be discouraged because the hon. member for Eed Deer has endeavoured to discourage the reading of history and the speeches and the lives of brilliant statesmen of the past. * Mr. MICHAEL CLARK: What I said was "forked lightning." I think you will agree with me, Sir, that I should not have words put into my mouth which I did not use. However, if the hon. member prefers the words "chain lightning " then he can employ them in the comparison.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The statement having been made this afternoon by the hon. member for Red Deer, the hon. member for Calgary should be allowed to reply by a similar statement. In deference to you, Mr. Chairman. I shall endeavour not to carry the analogy too far but just to the extent that it may appeal to the "intelligence" of the hon. member for Red Deer. Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. I do so not in the least because I object to anything my hon.

friend has said but because the Chair, for whom I have always displayed the utmost respect, has been openly defied.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I feel sure that the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) and the other hon. members of the committee will realise that if every hon. member in discussing this question went into the past history of every other hon. member to this same extent, it would be impossible to make any progress. I must once more respectfully ask him to bring his remarks to bear upon the question before the committee.

Without going into
the past history of the hon. gentleman, I would just say that once we were opposed, then we were united, and now the hon. member is with the National Progressive party. I am with the old party in which we were united. He has beaten me by one lap, which shows greater speed than I had ever dreamed of in my life. There are other instances which I would like to enter into but I feel the hour is getting late and perhaps the House is weary. But I want to point out to the hon. member for Red Deer that in connection with any business before the House I am perfectly willing to transact that business in the usual way, but I do not propose to take lectures from the hon. member in this House, or other persons. If we get a general understanding in this House that one man is not sent here to lecture any or all other members, we will make more rapid progress with the business of the country that is placed before us.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I wish to point out that the House and the country as a whole should be delighted that this discussion has taken place here to-day. It has shown that the Liberal party opposes the doctrine of the recall, advance resignations and agreements with committees. The supporters of the Government are opposed

to the recall, advance resignations and agreements with committees. Two men who spoke for the National Progressive party, of which there are some eight members in this House, repudiate the doctrine, and two more stand up and say that if they get GO or 75 per cent of the electors in their constituency to sign a petition for them to go home, they will go. There has not been one man stand up in this House to-day aud say that he believes in the advance resignation, that he believes in signing any agree- * ment limiting the performance of his duty as a member or that he believes in placing the control of his seat in this House in the hands of a few men.	_
Following the suggestion of the Acting Solicitor General, who has charge of the Bill and the suggestions of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen s and the leader of the Opposition, I shall be glad to withdraw this amendment and leave it to the further consideration of the Government.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is it the pleasure of
the committee that the hon. member have leave to withdraw his amendment?
No.

I wish to register my protest against an hon. member taking five . or six hours of our time for the entertainment and amusement of the House without having in any way mentioned the measure that is at present before us. I object to allowing this committee to be experimented with in that way. I believe the object of the hon. member (Mr. Tweedie) was to get the feeling of the House, and I am convinced that if he had expected that he would achieve any measure of success he would have pressed the question to a vote. He has either gone too far or he has not gone far enough. If it is worth while to have an expression of opinion it is worth while to have a division. [DOT] Then we will have a real expression. I might also point out another objection that I have to the proceeding that has taken place. Upon two or three nights during the present week, the hon. the Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Guthrie), who is in charge.of this Bill, has complained that its progress has been hindered by Opposition obstruction.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have never made such a complaint.

Well then I will
withdraw that remark and I will say that he has complained about the early rising of the committee. To-night when an hon.

gentleman who was speaking upon a matter that had no bearing upon this Bill at all, and was simply amusing the House, announced his intention of concluding his remarks, the minister called out, "go on; go on." Therefore, there is no sincerity at all in the statement of the minister that the Opposition are in any way lacking in a desire to proceed with public business, or that they are responsible for keeping the Bill before the House.
As the hon. member for West Calgary did not mention the amendment in my hearing to-night I do not understand why there is so much alarm about this recall. An organization outside of this House, one that has nothing to do with it, in its little union, or lodge, or whatever they call it, passes a resolution setting forth the principles upon which its members are willing to agree. I cannot see that in that there is anything that it is the business of this House to object to. If it were not for an agreement made by hon. gentlemen in 1917 there would not be any Union party to-day. Men came down here tied and bound by the conditions of an agreement which they had subscribed to, stipulating what they should do when they came here. I am not going to discuss that; I know it would not be in order but I would like to ask the Liberal Unionist members on the other side what their agreement was with the Union party?
Were the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) and the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) parties to that agreement?

I would think so. I did not enter into the agreement therefore I do not know what it is, but I read the platform of the Liberal Unionist party and it was stated that they had agreed to support the Government, and they appealed to the electors for that reason. Therefore they come down under exactly the same conditions with a pledge; the Farmer members come pledged to support the Farmers' platform. Many of them got a recall last winter, but they did not respond. In two or three constituencies, after they had failed to fulfil their agreement and were recalled, they did not stand for it.
In order that I may not be misunderstood I wish to say that I am not a member of that organization, but on the contrary have always been opposed by it. As far back as 1911 I was opposed by the Secretary of the United Farmers' Union, although the issue at that time was reciprocity. Their candidate ran as a third 131
man and opposed me although he stood on the same platform that I did. That gentleman signed a recall. I can remember the date on which he signed it, and the fact that half a dozen members of the organization went down and saw that the document was signed and sealed in the Merchants Bank in Vegreville-and I may say in passing that it is still there. So that the recall is not a dangerous thing, sometimes indeed it is very harmless. It is not a thing that will do harm to any one. It did not harm me in 1917 when 1 had a difficult election coming on and did not take the popular side on the questions at issue. Another man-a member of the same organization, in the person of Ex-Governor Leedy of Kansas-called himself a nonpartisan and stood on the same platform that I occupied as a supporter of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I think those people were the first to initiate the policy. ExGovernor Leedy had his recall all right but it did not affect my election. I think hon. gentlemen opposite-particularly the member for West Calgary and some of the other Western members-are being stampeded with the fear that possibly this organization is going to meet with so much success that it will be difficult for them to secure any seats in that part of the province. If that is the view they entertain I agree with them. I believe the movement will be successful. At the same time, I do not see why the farmers, or any class' of people, should not have the right to make conditions with their candidates the same as the Union Government did at the last general election. The Union Government at that time made an agreement with their candidates that they would support certain measures if elected. Perhaps, after all, those who are to blame for this movement are hon. gentlemen opposite, many of whom belonged to Farmers' organizations at the time of the last general election. At that time they told their electors that they only meant to support the Government on war measures, but that on the fiscal policy of the country and other questions they would adhere to the Farmers' platform. Many of them failed to carry out their promise, and perhaps it was for that reason that the recall plank was inserted in the Farmers* platform, so that in future when members do not live up to their pledges the people will have a right to recall them. My own opinion is that the opposition to it is merely an exemplification of the old Tory distrust of the people. They are afraid of the people. They drew]



this organization, which is growing all the time, and they are afraid to trust the people when the time comes for an election. They see something wrong about the Farmers' movement because these people band themselves together and pass by-laws that in my opinion have nothing to do with this Parliament. On several occasions this session I have noticed that when labour legislation, and other Bills of the same character were introduced, and the National Progressive members did not take part in the debate, attention was called to the fact and complaint was made that they did not support the measures in question, or else that they did object to some Bill. Criticism was levelled against them on both grounds. I think to-day's amendment is another example of the same policy. It has been introduced more with the idea of trying to draw out and get even with the members [DOT]of the Progressive party at the other end of the Chamber than from any other motive. As the leader of the Opposition has said: Let the people rule. If a majority of electors in any constituency are in ' favour of the recall they have a right to enter into any arrangement they may care to make with their representative. For my part, I have always been opposed to calling upon members to sign recalls. I do not suppose I shall ever be asked to sign such a thing altihoiugih there is very little difference 'between our party and tlheirs. The difference between us is of the nature that was described a few days ago by an hon. member when he remarked that on one occasion Lord Salisbury said that, "Gladstone was an old man in a hurry". II think the only difference between our friends at the other end of the Chamber and ourselves is that perhaps they are a little in a hurry. They are probably a little more advanced than we are, but they are standing on the same platform. We are pretty nearly agreed with them with the exception of what 'I may term these few "progressive" planks that have been adopted by them. The amendment of course has ibeen withdrawn-
No, no.

I should rather say the
request has been made that it should be withdrawn. I do' not think it is right that after so much valuable time has been taken up in discussing it ithe hon. member who moved the amendment should be allowed to withdraw it. The amendment should go to a vote in order that every member

of the committee might record where he stands.

I do not rise for the
purpose of continuing the debate on this question, but simply for the purpose of removing a misapprehension which I would gladly have done earlier if the minister (Mr. Guthrie) had displayed his usual courtesy and granted me an opportunity. On clause 101-Act to apply in elections under Canada Temperance Act:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada

speechtext: Does that mean that the lists will be prepared in each constituency as they are in a general election?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
In this case it will foe in the province instead of in the whole Domin-

ion, but the lists will be prepared in each constituency.

In preparing the lists for an ordinary election, the persons whose names may be placed on that list must have resided in Canada for twelve months prior to the issue of the writ. Will the provision in this case be that the residence in Canada shall he twelve months prior to the issue of the proclamation?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
That is made clear in the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I am opposed to the adoption of this clause, because it provides that the Act shall apply to elections held under the Canada Temperance Act. My view is that public moneys should not be expended in order to hold referendums in the various provinces on such questions as prohibition or prohibitory legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada

speechtext: My point is this: It is quite possible that the Canada Temperance Act may be repealed; it might even be repealed this year. I would like the minister either to suspend this clause or not to amend it so as to make it easier for provinces to come to the Dominion Government and ask for the use of federal funds every time they wish to hold a referendum or to change their mii^ds with reference to prohibition or prohibitory legislation. As I understand it, the minister's point of order is that we have so amended the Canada Temperance Act as to provide that referendums may be held under it, and that 'these shall be governed by the Dominion Elections Act. To that I reply that it is not within our province to make it easier, by the provisions of this Act, for the local legislatures or local bodies to hold any such referendums. If the minister's point of order is well taken, then I *may not proceed; if it is not, I shall proceed to discuss the matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Any discussion of the results of the application of any province to the Federal Government for a referendum under the Canada Temperance Act would not be in order upon this clause.

With .further reference to what the hon. member (Mr. Powct) has 131i
said, I do not wish to get in conflict with your decision, Mr. Chairman; I simply wish to direct the attention of the minister to the following facts. The Temperance Act is either complete or it is not. If it is complete, it must contain provisions for the taking of referendums; if it is not complete, it ought to be completed.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That, of course, may be done by another Act.

Exactly. Why put in the electoral law of Canada a clause which has exclusive relation to the Canada Temperance Act? This clause ought to be inserted in the Canada Temperance Act, not in the Franchise Act.
I think the hon. member (Mr. Cannon) is absolutely right in his contention. This clause should be put in the Canada Temperance Act, not here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Canada Temperance Act itself provides that the persons who shall be entitled to vote under it are such persons as would be entitled to vote at a Dominion election held on the day of the plebiscite under the Temperance Act. Now, this Act .simply says that the provisions which apply to everybody who is entitled to vote at a Dominion election shall apply in the case of a vote taken under the Canada Temperance Act. It is simply meeting the express provision of the Canada Temperance Act.

The remarks of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) complete my remarks. I said that the Canada Temperance Act was either complete or incomplete. The minister tell us that it is complete. Therefore, this clause is useless.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not say that; I said that this, clause completes it.

If the Canada Temperance Act says that the referendum is to be taken according to the provisions of the Dominion Elections Act, why put this clause into the Dominion Elections Act having reference to the Canada Temperance Act? The clause in the Canada Temperance Act, of which the Minister of Justice has just spoken, renders this clause without any purpose or use.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When that enactment was made in the Canada Temperance Act, there was then an Act of the Dominion of Canada, determining who it was that voted at the elections for this Parliament held under that Act; and .the Canada Temper-

ance Act, taking the existing condition of things, enacted that persons entitled under then existing legislation to vote at a Dominion election would he entitled to vote under the Canada Temperance Act. We are changing the whole law governing who is to vote at Dominion elections-, and the purpose of the provision under discussion is simply to make it clear that, as this measure changes the class of persons entitled to vote and the provisions with regard to voting at Dominion -elections, it -shall in the future apply for the purpose of implementing -and carrying out that express provision o-f the Canada Temperance Act.

Then, I submit that the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) had a right to raise the question he raised. When the Canada Temperance Act was enacted and provisions were made for a referendum to he taken, the provincial lists were to 'be used for the purpose of taking that referendum. With this new clause in this Bill, neiw lists will have to be prepared -for the special purpose of taking that referendum, and the cost of that ,will -be paid (by this Government. That means -that if the Provincial Government of Ontario- take a referendum, lists will be prepared under this Bill that will co-st, perhaps, $500,000, and that amount will he paid by this country. As I -stated before, ,when the Canada Temperance Act was passed, it was not contemplated that we should have- to prepare special lists as will have to be prepared under clause 101. I think my hon. friend (Mr. Power) was right in complaining that such a tremendous cost -should be forced upon this country. If the province of Ontario or any other province -wants to take a referendum this year, or next year, or the following year, let that province pay for it. I am certainly in order, and my ho-n. friend (Mr. Power) was in order, in- opposing this clause on that ground.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think there is anything to he gained by so doing; but if my hon. friend wants to let this clause stand until clause 32 has been discussed and passed, I am quite agreeable.
Section 101 stands.

On section 29-qualification of electors:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Some days ago I gave notice that, when this clause was considered,
I would move an amendment. I, therefore, move to amend clause 29 by adding, as paragraph (d) of subclause 1, the following words:
(d) Provided, however, that any Indian ordinarily resident on an Indian Reserve who has served in the naval, military or air forces of Canada in the late war shall be qualified to vote, unless such Indian is otherwise disqualified under paragraphs (a) (b) and (c) of this section.
How could he be "otherwise disqualified"?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: He might not have the residential and age qualifications, for instance.
Is the idea that the man who has served in the army or navy and is not twenty-one has not the right to vote? He is disfranchised?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Under the amendment I have proposed the Indian who has served with the forces would only be entitled to vote when he complies with all the -other requisites in regard to British citizenship, residence and age.
Why limit it to Indians who are ordinarily resident on a reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Indians who are living on a reserve and who are receiving the bounty of the Government are the wards of the Government and they have nearly always been disqualified under our Dominion Franchise Acts.

But there are Indians who are not living on a reserve, and they have no right to vote unless they are enfranchised. There are many Indians who are working and living outside the reserve. They have no right to vote at the present time, but why shouldn't they vote if they have served in the army or navy?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Any Indian not ordinarily resident on an Indian reserve is entitled to vote provided he has the other qualifications.
When he is on a reserve he will not vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If he is ordinarily resident on an Indian reserve he will not vote.
Why?	*

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Because he is looked on as a ward of the Government.

I am rather in favour of this clause. I think that any person who
is in receipt of assistance from the Government, or who can be influenced by the Government, ought not to have the right to vote. It is an easy matter to see how they would vote if they had that right.

What about an Indian who has served with the forces and who is not resident on an Indian reserve, but lives outside at a nearby village? Near Quebec there is an Indian reserve at Lorette. Some of the Indians live on the reserve, but others who are emancipated live in the village of Lorette outside.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They are not disqualified under this clause.

Under the amendment an Indian requires two essential qualifications in order to vote. First, he must have served in the army or navy or with the air forces, and secondly, he must be ordinarily resident on an Indian reserve.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Off the reserve.
Suppose an Indian had served in the late war and lived on a reservation, would he be entitled to vote?

The amendment reads:
Provided, however, that any Indian ordinarily resident on an Indian Reserve who has served in the Naval, Military or Air forces of Canada in the late war shall be qualified to vote.
The minister said the amendment read: "Not ordinarily resident." Which is right?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It seems to be so simple as not to need explanation. A man-is qualified to vote, not being an Indian ordinarily resident on an Indian reserve. The meaning of that is that an Indian who is ordinarily resident on a reserve has no vote. But if such an Indian residing on a reserve served in the army or navy or air forces he will have the right to vote provided he has the other qualifications.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Unless there is some special disfranchising Act. This Act does not disqualify him. This Act only disfranchises an Indian ordinarily resident on an Indian reserve. I know of no other disfranchising Act. It may be that the Indian Act provides that an Indian in receipt of bounty shall not vote, but I am not sure about that.

My hon. friend (Mr. Cannon) is absolutely right. The Act provides that an Indian ordinarily resident on an Indian reserve who has served in the army or navy or air forces shall have the right to vote, but there is nothing here giving the right to vote to a man who does not reside on a reserve but has served with the forces.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: He does not need it. He is not disqualified. There is nothing in the Act that will disqualify a man who does not reside on a reserve.
He may be a member of the band, subject to all the rules of the band, and live outside the reserve.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There is nothing in this Act that disqualifies him.

As the law stands now, under the Indian Act an Indian is absolutely disfranchised. An Indian, to cease to be an Indian, has to be emancipated or enfranchised under the procedure laid down in the Indian Act. If that procedure has not been followed, and if the Indian has served in the late war and does not reside on an Indian reserve but in a nearby village the amendment does not give him the right to vote, I think he ought to have it. We have a reserve at Lorette near Quebec. Some members of the tribe live on the reserve and others in the village. Those living in the village have no right to vote unless they are enfranchised. I know that some of the members of this tribe have served in the war. By this amendment they would not be entitled to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This Act is pretty specific in its provisions. I am not sure what is in the Indian Act, but I am inclined to think from what I have heard around me that there is some disqualification in that Act of an Indian who is in receipt of money from the Government. They are looked on as wards of the Government. This Act won't interfere with them. There is no disqualification in this Act except of the Indian ordinarily resident on a reserve, and even they have the right to vote if they have served with the forces and are not otherwise disqualified. If he resides off the reserve he is not disqualified under this Act.
Yes he is, unless he is enfranchised.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If he is off the reserve this Act does not disqualify him. It only disqualifies the Indian on the reserve.

But the Indian off the reserve i! disqualified by law until he is enfranchised. At the present time we have a Committee of this House studying the whole Indian question, and some members of the Committee are in favour of compulsorily enfranchising the Indians who live off the reserve because they are no longer wards of the Government. There are certain disabilites; they cannot be sued for debt, and so on. 'So my hon. friend is wrong when he says the Indians living off the reserve will have the right to vote. They will have that right only when they are enfranchised under the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Any disability is not under this Act; it is under the Indian Act. -
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The other Act may be amended when the House sees fit to amend it. There is no disability under this Act except as against Indians who live on the reserve.
Why not strike out the words "Indian ordinarily resident on an Indian reserve."
I think there is something in the Indian Act which provides that unless an Indian renounces his tribal allegiance he has no vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If he does renounce his tribal allegiance and then goes back to the reserve he cannot vote under this section.
Is an Indian who was not enfranchised but who served in the war and is now living off the reservation, entitled to vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Not if the Indian Act says not.
Why not? If an Indian served in the war and is thus entitled to vote, why should he not vote, whether he lives on or off the reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps we had better look at the Indian Act; we have so many different opinions.

The minister says, and this Act provides, that the man who is ordinarily resident on an Indian reservation and who has served with the air or military forces shall be entitled to vote.
'Mr. GUTHRIE: Yes.
If a man is not ordinarily resident on a reservation, what is his status?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: He can vote anywhere.
No, not unless he is enfranchised.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This Act declares that he shall have the vote.

No, it does not declare that. Only the man ordinarily resident on the reservation shall vote. Now, why should the man who is not on the reservation but who served in the war not be entitled to vote? That is the point.
Mr. HARO'LD: This point must be made clear. When our committee was sitting, we had before us Lieut. Martin, of Toronto. He is at present living in that city and has not a vote ordinarily because he is attached to the band and is not enfranchised. I think, therefore, that this amendment should cover those. Indians off the reservation.
Exactly.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I move to strike out of the amendment the words " ordinarily resident on an Indian reserve."
Will the minister consider giving the vote to the wives of the Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No; we give the Indians the vote only because of their war service.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I move to amend clause 29 by adding to the said clause the following words:
Provided that no disability imposed by paragraph (b) of subsection 4 of section 8 of "The Naturalization Act", chapter thirty-eight of the statutes of 1919 (first session), shall disentitle a person on that ground alone to the said certificate.

When the principle of this clause was discussed on the second reading of the Bill some weeks ago and it was realized that the clause, when read with a certain clause in the Naturalization Act, would disfranchise probably one hundred thousand British subjects, I was very much gratified to hear the pronouncement from the Government, through the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen), that it was not the intention of the Government that there should be such an effect, and further that an amendment would be introduced later on that would remove the injustice. That amendment is now before us, and I may say frankly, Mr. Chairman, that I believe that a better remedy would have consisted in striking
out that part of the clause altogether. I shall speak of that very briefly a little later. It is impossible to discuss the amendment intelligently without discussing to some extent at least the Naturalization Act. Indeed, I think there is even now in the House, and perhaps throughout the country, a very considerable misconception as to the purport of the Bill as it stands _ and of this amendment as it is now proposed. There are two groups of people who have been discussed in connection with this Bill, and the reason for that is to be found in the Naturalization Act that was passed last year, particularly section 8. I have no desire to transgress the rules, but I think it is necessary that I should make some reference to the Naturalization Act in connection with this subject. In section 8 of that Act provision was made that no persons of enemy alien origin could be naturalized in Canada without living in this country for ten years after the conclusion of peace. That provision embraced people who had lived in Canada for a great many years, and I discussed that question at the time and made an objection to the principle of applying that provision to men who had lived in this country for so many years, many of whom had considered themselves British subjects and many of whom had voted in the past. However, it was said at the time that it was necessary to draft the clause in that form because of the requirements of the British Government, who desired that all certificates issued in the future by the Canadian Government should carry with them Imperial naturalization. It was also promised by the Prime Minister at that time that he would make representations to the British Government to have that matter modified. That has not as yet been done, but I understand from interviews with certain members of the Government that application has been made to the British Government and that action may be expected. I should like to say, by the way, that if that cannot be obtained I would suggest to the Government that in all fairness they should introduce some legislation whereby these people might be given, if not Imperial naturalization, at least Canadian naturalization, which would meet the requirements of nine hundred and ninety-nine out of a thousand of those who would like (Canadian naturalization to peirmit them to vote. This would be all the more reasonable, because we know as a matter of fact to-day that the man in Canada who was formerly an enemy alien, or at least
!058

who was born in Germany or Austria and who has Canadian naturalization, finds it absolutely impossible to get the Imperial naturalization certificate even though he served in the war. If these people could get Canadian naturalization that would remedy the matter, as far as the franchise is concerned.
The amendment as proposed does not affect those people of enemy alien origin who cannot be naturalized for another ten years. I think there is an impression throughout the country-I know I have met with it in my own constituency-that by this amendment all those who cannot be naturalized until they have lived in Canada for ten years will now he able to vote. I think it should be made perfectly clear that people who have not been naturalized are not affected by this amendment at all, and that it only deals with those who are British subjects by operation of law. The people who are spoken of as British subjects by operation of law are those who are naturalized by reason of the naturalization of their fathers, in the case of children and minors, or those who are naturalized by reason of the naturalization of their husbands in the case of the wives of these men. In the Bill as it was presented these people would have been prevented from voting and I think, with the exception of one point that I desire to bring out briefly, the amendment as proposed by the Acting Solicitor General will make it possible under certain conditions that these people now receive the franchise.
The point I wish to raise is a legal one, and perhaps it may seem somewhat presumptuous for one who is not a lawyer to raise it. It is a point that I discussed with the Acting Solicitor General. He did not think there was any force in it. I discussed it with certain other members of the House who are learned in the law, some on this side and one or two on the other side, and in order that the opinion which I myself have on the point might be supported or otherwise by someone who could not in any way be considered a partisan, I drew it to the attention of a gentleman who has a great deal to do with matters of this kind in connection with naturalization and discussed it with him. That was the Under Secretary of State, Mr. Thomas Mulvey. When I placed it before him and asked him for his opinion, he said that the meaning which I took out of it was correct, and that at the very best it would be doubtful whether under certain sections of the Naturalization Act the right to vote which

would be given by the amendment now proposed, would not again be taken away. I am bringing the point out now, not for the purpose of raising any objection but simply to make absolutely certain that the declared intention of the Government to give the franchise to these people shall be carried out.
The point is as follows: Under section 29, which we are now discussing, a certificate may be given to those British subjects who are British subjects by operation of the law. The certificate is given to:
Every person who is naturalized as a British subject by operation of law who, but for such naturalization, is qualified and would be entitled at the date of this certificate to be personally naturalized in Canada.
For these hundred thousand people who are naturalized by operation of law it will be necessary, before they can vote, to go before a judge and prove to him that they are qualified for personal naturalization. They are not required, as I take it, to actually secure that personal naturalization, but they must have the qualification before he can issue a certificate to that effect which certificate gives them the right to vote. In the Naturalization Act, section 5, subsection 3, there is the following clause:
Except as provided by this Act, a certificate of naturalization shall not be granted to any person under disability.
The word "disability" is defined in section 33 paragraph (d) as follows:
The expression "disability" means the status of being a married woman, or a minor, lunatic or idiot.
What I have particular reference to in this connection is that the expression "disability" means the status of being a married woman. In the Act itself there appears to be no provision whatever for the personal naturalization of a married woman who is already a British subject, because her husband is a naturalized British subject. Therefore it would seem that when such a woman appeared before the judge and asked for a certificate which would give 'her the right to vote the judge would very naturally say to her that he is not entitled to issue a certificate of personal naturalization because there is no provision for the naturalization of a married woman who is already a British subject by operation of law.
The Acting Solicitor General did not agree with that view, as I have said before, and I have no doubt he will place his view on that point before the committee. If there is anything in it at all, the amend-

ment which has been offered by him should be so framed that all possible doubt will be removed and that the object that is sought to be attained by the amendment will be fully carried out, and so that those who are British subjects by operation of law will find there is no obstacle placed in the way of their obtaining certificates and being allowed to vote.
I said a few moments ago, Mr. Chairman, that in my opinion the best remedy would be to strike the paragraph out altogether. It would make it very much more simple, there could be no doubt whatever about it, and it would base the franchise broadly upon the fact of British citizenship, which seems altogether fair and which would carry out the principle enunciated by the Acting Solicitor General himself when he introduced the Bill in the first place.
The point I want to make is that people affected by the amendment are already British subjects, and while I have no fault to find with the principle that is sought to be enacted here, that every alien should receive personal naturalization, it does not seem to me to be altogether fair that the principle should be made retroactive and that you should force British subjects, many of whom have voted in the past, to again appear before a judge in order that they may obtain a certificate. Indeed the chief objection that I have to that is this: I think it is altogether likely that in a great many instances these people will not appear before the judge, for various reasons. One of these reasons might quite conceivably be a certain matter of pride. For example take the case of the men who may have voted for ten or fifteen years, ever since they came of age, and who were naturalized because their fathers were naturalized.
