I do not see why these men should be placed in a separate class and again be asked to prove that they are fit for citizenship and for the exercise of the franchise; it seems to me they might very-well be excused from that. Again, I believe it is altogether probable that in many cases the names of these people- wives of naturalized British subjects, and men naturalized by operation of law-will be placed on the voters' lists, and they will assume that they are entitled to vote. They will take no further trouble in connection with the matter. They will appear at the polls, and then it may be quite possible that somebody will object, will ask them for the certificate, and as they will not have it, they will be deprived of the franchise at that time. It seems to me that that should be avoided.
It would be quite fair, I think, that the law might apply to all newcomers or those who are naturalized in the future, but that it should be made retroactive, it seems to me, is not fair at all. I would ask the Government in that connection not to have their amendment stop short of giving complete justice to these people, but to strike out the paragraph altogether, and let the franchise be the inseparable and logical accompaniment of mature citizenship, and give the vote to all who are British subjects of the proper age.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The question raised by my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) is not without some complexity. Under the Bill as originally introduced- clause 29, subclause 2-the intention of the Government in framing the clause was hardly expressed by the language used, as was pointed out on the second reading of the Bill by the Minister of the Interior. The effect of the clause as originally drawn, and now printed in the Bill, would be to disqualify a certain number of people in this country who had heretofore become British subjects by operation of law. The people who would have been thus disqualified, were the section allowed to remain in its present condition, were the wives and children of those who had come to this country from foreign countries and obtained naturalization in Canada during their minority. As the committee is well aware, the wife of an alien who becomes naturalized in this country, under our law, becomes a British subject. The wife did not have to appear and obtain the certificate of naturalization-she became a British subject by operation of law by the fact of her marriage. Under the old common law idea she merged her existence, her identity became merged in her husband, and by operation of law she became a British subject. So it was also with the children who were minors at the time the parent became a British subject. Not so with the children who had come to the age of twenty-one years. They retained their original citizenship until they should themselves apply for naturalization in this country. My hon. friend from North Waterloo was, I think, the first to point out, during the debate on the second reading of this Bill, that the clause as drawn, had the effect of depriving a certain number of British subjects of the right to the franchise. The Minister of the Interior very promptly informed the House that such was not intended-that if that were the interpretation of the language of the section it did not convey the intention of the Government-and

and distant past did obtain naturalization certificates which have since become lost or destroyed, or the records in connection with which have become obliterated. At all events, we have at the present time in various ridings in Ontario very old and very worthy people of German descentpossibly of Austrian descent, too

who
cannot establish the fact that they are British subjects. They may say that they have voted for twenty, thirty or forty years. I have personal knowledge of some instances, because the admission was made to me, in which men who had voted had never been naturalized.
It has been argued that these people should not now be deprived of the right to be naturalized, though in section 8 of our Naturalization Act we have adopted the Imperial clause' that provides that people of a former alien enemy state shall not be entitled to naturalization for ten years after the conclusion of peace. The situation is not a happy one; but it is one that has arisen, I think, largely on account of lack of interest or carelessness of the individuals themselves who did not see to it in years gone by that they were properly naturalized, or who were so careless in regard to the matter that the records became lost or the certificates were destroyed and they are unable to establish the fact now. The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) makes a suggestion to meet the difficulty; he made it last session. He has made it, I think, privately to the Prime Minister (Sir .Robert Borden), and his request has been promised, and has received, consideration. His proposal is this: That we in Canada have still the power to pass a Canadian Naturalization Act and that we should pass a Canadian Naturalization Act and by that means give these people the Canadian franchise. The matter has, however, assumed more than a Canadian aspect. We have passed an Imperial Naturalization Act which gives us the right to confer upon the people of this country citizenship throughout the British Empire. We passed that Act with our eyes open, making it on all fours with Acts passed in the other British Dominions. We passed it deliberately after a long experience during which we granted Canadian citizenship after three years' residence in this country, good only within Canada, and such a Canadian citizen who left Canada was not a British subject. In fact, I am told that high dignitaries of this country went as representatives of this country to Great Britain and found when they got there that

they were not British subjects, simply because they had only Canadian naturalization. Now a man who gets a certificate of naturalization in this country, is justified in believing that he is a British subject throughout the British Empire. My hon. friend (Mr. Euler) says: You have it in your power to give Canadian naturalization. Deliberately, we rejected that old system and adopted a new one; we placed ourselves on a par with the other Dominions and the Motherland herself, and that was done after full consideration of all the circumstances. I think it was last session that the Prime Minister promised my hon. friend that he would fully consider the matter and take it up with the Imperial authorities. Doubtless the failure of his health and his consequent absence from this country prevented him from doing so personally although he started the negotiations. I am able, however, to tell the committee that the negotiations have proceeded, but they have not proceeded to that extent that the Government is able to announce that an arrangement has yet been reached.
I do not know if a satisfactory arrangement can be looked for in the near future. Personally, I am inclined to think this is one of the matters that may be discussed at the Imperial Conference to be held in 1921, although I cannot give the committee any more than my opinion in that regard. It is certain that up to the present moment we have not received the assent of Great Britain to that proposal. Shall we deliberately derogate from our own Act and create a new status after having deliberately overthrown the old status and accepted the Imperial one? I do not think it will be a very long time for us to wait until we have a final decision. It may be that there will not be any great necessity for voting in the interval; I hope there will not, but as to that no one can speak with any confidence. That, however, is the situation. The object of the present amendment is to make definite and certain that every one who is actually a British subject shall enjoy the right to vote, and if the amendment that I have moved does not make that clear, we shall make it clear if a better method can be suggested.

Who will be the persons, British subjects by operation of the law, who will remain disqualified or who will be unable to obtain a certificate entitling them to vote under this clause as amended? Will there remain any such persons?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No one who is a British subject.
Then, what is the purpose of subclause 2 of clause 29 if every person will be able to vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not quite catch my hon. friend's meaning.
I want to know who are those who will be unable to obtain a certificate giving them the right to vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Those who could not go personally and get naturalized; those who depend only on their marriage or their parentage could not obtain naturalization under subclause 2.
In that class will be included those who do not have a good knowledge of the English or the French language.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That would be a disqualification. Any one who could not comply with the qualifications of our Naturalization Act, which include a knowledge of either the French or the English language, would be disqualified.

Might I ask the Acting
Solicitor General, in opening, if those who were aliens and who had already become naturalized prior to the Nautralization Act of 1919, are stdl entitled to vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: A male?
Yes. He became naturalized prior to the Naturalization Act of 1919. Is he still entitled to vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I shall have to examine the clauses of the Naturalization Act as>
to that. I have them before me, but I have not time to examine them just now. It may be there is some discretion. He would have formerly one of the limited certificates, good only in Canada. My hon. friend Tefers only as to the vote, not as to obtaining Imperial citizenship?

I am speaking only in
regard to the right to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, he can vote, but
he has to make a new application if he desires to get an Imperial certificate, or a certificate under the Act of 1919.

But in order to vote at
any succeeding election, he has not to get a new certificate, provided that he was naturalized1 prior to 1919, even though that Naturalization Act was passed in that year?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think there is any doubt that a man who has heretofore been naturalized1 under the law of this country as that law stood at the time of the issue of his certificate, has a right to vote, and his wife would be a British subject according to law.
Would she have a right to vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. Unless she were
a person born in North America, she would have to apply to a judge to show that she would have a right to vote, to get a certificate.

Even though the husband is entitled to vote owing to naturalization prior to the Naturalization Act of 1919 and his wife thereby became a British subject prior to 1919, the husband would not have to apply again and would be entitled to vote, but the wife would have to apply for a new certificate?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
No, she would have to
apply to the judge, before voting, for a certificate under this clause., [DOT]

In other words; although she became a British subject by operation of law, owing to the fact that her husband was naturalized prior to the Naturalization Act of 1919 and is still a British subject for the purpose of the franchise, his wife would still have to obtain a certificate in order to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, it is to meet her case that this clause was drawn.

But this would have no
bearing at all on the man himself?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No.

I ask the Acting Solicitor General these questions by reason of the fact that the other day I received from a very eminent barrister, who has had much to do with the naturalization of these people, a latter in which he states:
The Government of Canada in 1917 took cognizance of the fact that there were many aliens who had resided in Canada for many years whose sympathies were with the United Kingdom as its Allies in the Great War and who had no Pro-German or other alien affiliations. This fact was officially recognized particularly in Orders in Council No. 2552 and No. 2948. Thereupon the Department of the Secretary of State published in pamphlet form the Naturalization Act of 1914 with Amendments, the Orders in Council and the departmental regulations applicable to naturalization.
The Act and the regulations prescribed all the steps necessary to be taken by an alien in order to perfect his naturalization. He was told that he must post up a notice, a*** Gutnish cer-

tain facts, and attend before the clerk of the Court to sign a petition, and then, finally, appear before the County Judge and give evidence to show that he had qualified under the Act.
The Orders in Council, the Regulations and the pamphlet freely distributed practically constituted an invitation to those who came within the meaning of the Act to come forward and become British subjects and Canadian citizens. Scores responded to the invitation. In the county of Grey about one hundred and fifty made application. I dealt with a number of these applications myself. Looking over these applications I see that some of them came to Canada in infancy; some at the age of four or five years; I believe that the majority of them came -when under ten years of age ; few came after twenty years of age; some of them had lived in Canada for sixty years; they practically knew no other country; ninety per cent of these men were told by the politicians of the day that they were qualified to vote if they would only swear that they were British subjects and they were told that all that was necessary was to take the oath of allegiance. Not knowing any better they believed that they were British .subjects and voted as such at every election. They occupied positions of municipal trust, took a general interest in Canadian affairs and lived irreproachable lives so far as law and order are concerned. When the war broke out they were more or less opposed to Germany because the parents of many of these men had left Germany t<f avoid the burden of military service.
These men followed diligently the regulations prescribed by'the department, engaged counsel and paid the fees prescribed by the Government, and to that extent enriched the Treasury, attended at the County Town once or twice and incurred expenses in connection with their naturalization varying from $25 to $35.
The applications were heard by the County Judges. Those who, in the opinion of the County Judge, who, from his local knowledge is best able to ascertain the1 facts, gave satisfactory evidence had their applications approved. Those who did not satisfy him were rejected.
A very large number of these applications were heard at the end of June 1919. Two weeks afterwards, on the 7th of July, 1919, the present Naturalization Act became law and these applicants, who had been for months making their applications, found that certificates would not be granted for a further period of ten years when the majority of them would be in their graves.
I need hardly say that solicitors who, like myself, had prepared the applications for these men and advised them as to the steps to take and the circumstances under which certificates would be granted, resent very strongly being placed in the position of taking fees from these men and then, owing to the Act of 1919, being compelled to advise them that the whole procedure was a farce and that they have lost their -money.
One County Judge referred to it as a scandal and all who were concerned in putting through these applications feel that we were placed in a false position.
That is the opinion expressed by a very eminent Canadian barrister. Now are these men who had obtained these certificates prior to the Naturalization Act of 1919 still entitled, as they were before, irrespective

of the ten-year clause in the 1919 Naturalization Act, to vote under the present Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no doubt about it,, if they obtained their certificates. I am speaking of the naturalization certificate under the law as it stood prior to the passing of the 1919 Act.
Mr. CiA'LDER: There must be a naturalization certificate from the Secretary of State.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: A certificate that complied with the law as it then stood.
So that any man who appeared before the county judge and was deemed fit for naturalization would be entitled to vote under the present Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think he would be naturalized, under the 1914 Act.
Prior to 1919, complying with the law as it then was.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend looks at the 1914 Act he will find differently I think.

All the applicant had to do was this. He had to go before any barrister, preferably the County Crown Attorney, and prove if he was foreign born, that he had a residence of three years in Canada, then make his petition, then make his affidavit that he would file that petition, and give notice of application for naturalization for three months before the sittings of the county court sessions, and then become naturalized. What I want to know is this: Are those men who received their naturalization certificates from the County Crown Attorney, through the medium of being naturalized by the high court judge o.r a judge of the sessions, entitled to vote under the Act as it stands?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.
What have they got to do?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They are not entitled because they did not get certificates of naturalization.
They did.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Let me point out what they got. The judge, under the Act of 1914, gives hobody a certificate of naturalization, but a certificate that the applicant has satisfied him, the judge, that he has the necessary qualifications to be naturalized. That certificate of the judge is not a

certificate that he is naturalized, but a certificate that he has the necessary qualifications. That certificate has to go to the Secretary of State, and upon that certificate the Secretary of State may issue the certificate of naturalization. He is under no obligation to issue it. On the contrary, he has an absolute discretion,, and a man has never got his naturalization certificate until he gets it from the Secretary of State. The Secretary of State can grant it, and nobody else.
That is since 1914?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. The judge intervenes simply as the instrument to gather the necessary evidence and forward to the Secretary of State the certificate that he has satisfied himself that the man has the qualifications. The people to whom my hon. friend refers are entitled to every sympathy, but unfortunately, as the situation is described, if all they got before the last Naturalization Act came into force was the certificate that emaninated from the judge, they did not get their certificate of naturalization and apparently this legislation of 1919 operated to hold the hand of the Secretary of State and prevent his issuing certificates of naturalization.

Taking what the Minister of Justice (Mr/ Doherty) isays, it means that those who had received naturalization prior to 1914 by certificate of the judge are not under this Act entitled to vote, and by reason of the Naturalization Act of 1914, they will yet have to wait four years before they are entitled to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The man who before
1914, or in fact,, for three years after 1914, got naturalized under the old Act-under the old Act the judge naturalized; he gave his certificate of naturalization and that was the end of the operation, for his certificate was the certificate of naturalization -was a naturalized British subject in Canada, and the later legislation did not take away from him What he already had.
But it is taken away.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The man who was
naturalized under the Act in force prior to 1914, and which for people who had come into the country before 1914 remained in force for a further period of nearly three years, got naturalization in Canada alone, but he still has that thing that he got. So far as he personally is concerned his rights, so far as I know, are not affected by the legislation of 1919.
He is still entitled to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I was dealing with the case which the hon. member for West Lambton put forward, of the man who was cut off by the passing of the legislation of 1919. It is perfectly true that during the war the issuing of certificates under the legislation of 1914 to persons of alien enemy nationality was suspended.
Why, then, (were Orders in Council, providing for such naturalization, passed during the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When you say "Orders in Council," it is difficult to know precisely to what particular Orders in Council you refer. There were certain Orders in Council, looking to the particular eases of people who had been long periods of years in the country, and providing for exceptions to the general suspension that had been decided upon of the issuing of naturalization certificates to persons of alien enemy nationality during the war. Orders in

Council were passed making it possible to create exceptions. But such exceptions were not given effect to under those Orders in Council, because it (was found essential to the general safety of the Empire that, while the war was actually in progress, there should be no grants of naturalization to people of enemy nationality. That view was so strongly pressed and insisted upon that it was thought justifiable, notwithstanding that Orders in Council were passed, not to grant certificates while the war was on.
Do I understand the minister to say that there were actually no certificates of naturalization granted to people who had been born in Germany for example? Does he say that no exceptions were made?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not in a position to say that there was absolutely no exception made; I would have to verify that statement. But the general practice which the hon. member was complaining of was that certificates were njot granted. Now, whether there were one or more cases that were considered absolutely exceptional I am not in a position to say. The administration of the Act was not in my personal control but in the Department of the Secretary of State, and I am not in a position to answer that question. I was trying to explain to the hon. gentleman how it happened that though there were Orders in Council looking to the making of exceptions, on general principles certificates have not been granted and those Orders in Council have not been generally carried out. I cannot say that, during the course of the war there were not possibly some cases so exceptional as to justify the granting of certificates.

Are those who were not naturalized prior to 1914 or 1919 and who had lived in this country for forty years, entitled to become naturalized, or must they wait for ten years?
Mr; GUTHRIE: If they came from what we know as alien enemy countries they must wait for ten years.
Even though they may have lived here forty years?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Even so.

Then I want to make a strong protest against such an invidious restriction being incorporated in this statute. I do not believe it will be in the interests of the country. I have very strong sentiments in connection with the war and the

duties of citizenship, but it does appear to me that after all has been said and done, we should try as far as possible to get away from the war spirit and try to build the nation on the new principles which the war has taught us. Is it right that we should say to people, of whom undoubtedly there are large numbers in this country, that although they came here in order to get away as far as possible from the conditions that existed in their own countries; although they left their native land to avoid unjust and autocratic forcing into military service, coming to this country to seek peace and (quietness and happiness and to contribute to the wealth of their adopted land by their thrift and economy,- is it fair that we should say to them that, notwithstanding the .fact that they are good citizens, they shall be deprived of the rights of citizenship? No one knows better than the Acting Solicitor General that if you go up into these very sections where the largest percentage of these people live- and I can speak for Ontario-you will find men and women than whom there are no more thrifty, energetic, honest, law-abiding, God-fearing people anywhere. Yet, we are going to say to those people- Although you left your country many years ago, when you were mere children, and came here to escape the tyranny of your own country; although you have proved yourselves good citizens, having added to the wealth of this country, having paid your taxes, yet, by reason of a hard-and-fast law passed in this Parliament that recognizes nothing in mitigation of the accident of your birth, you are to be deprived of the right to have a single word to say in the government of your country. It does appear to me, and I want to speak as calmly and reasonably as possible, that in forcing such .a measure through, the Government is only making trouble for itself in the future and creating .a schism which ought not to exist, The whole civilized world to-day, .now that the war is over, is trying to forget the past few years and to allay bitter hatred and animosity, yet we are attempting to open old wounds in Canada to-day. I say that this is bad legislation. It is an enactment that ought to be very seriously and carefully considered before it is passed. I care not one whit as to what ,the provisions of Imperial citizenship may be.
It has been said: You cannot derogate from your own Act. In so far as Canada is concerned, the Parliament of Canada is the only one to say who shall and who

shall not vote for the representatives of this country. I do not want to take away from that to the extent of one iota. We are practically, in that respect, masters of our owh destiny. We should not pass that legislation, leave that schism, that breach, for a period of ten years and practically segregate a large portion of the people. The Acting Solicitor General has said, it is not a happy situation. I absolutely agree with him. It is 'a distinctly unhappy situation. It is not only an unhappy situation, but it is a situation that the Government is making more unhappy. Why could we not wipe out that Naturalization Act in effect by this Act? The Minister of Justice shakes his head. I suppose he means that we cannot wipe out that Naturalization Act without consent. I know not why. Surely we in this Parliament have power to repeal an Act that -we have passed. If we cannot do that, the sooner we know it the better. With Canada's status to-day-and with Canada's status I thoroughly agree-if we cannot, in our own House, run our own internal affairs, or make our statutes and declare who shall be entitled to return representatives for making the laws and looking after the affairs of this country without the consent of some one else, the sooner we know it the better.
I make the appeal very earnestly, I feel sincerely about it, and I am doing it for no political purpose whatever. This is an Act which will only redound to the discredit, and not to the benefit of Canada. I therefore think that w'e should so amend this Act, section 29 of the Bill, that the classes whom I have mentioned shall be entitled to vote. They have shown themselves to be good citizens and they are the victims of a condition for which they are not in the least responsible. Although they are thrifty, although they are God-fearing, although they are doing their best to upbuild Canada and promote its prosperity, shall we say, merely by reason of the accident of birth: <sWe will have none of you. You may pay your taxes, we will take your money, but as to you having a voice in the affairs of this nation, away with you." That is not good policy. It is not a policy that is going to build up and bring about the unity and cohesion of the people of Canada. The Government that passes that legislation and adheres to it is not acting in the interest of the people of Canada. It may be acting for a section of the people. The Government that passes that legislation will yet rue it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let me point out to the hon. gentleman that he did not quite grasp the point that I disagreed with him upon, although I am not prepared to say that I can endorse everything he said. The hon. gentleman says that the Act that we are dealing with now is taking the franchise away from these people. That is a mistake. This Act is giving the franchise to every British subject, with restrictions that have no hearing upon the matter at present under consideration. The difficulty that arises in the path of those on whose behalf the hon. gentleman has spoken with such force and eloquence is not to be found in this Act.
No, it is in the Naturalization Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is in the Naturalization Act.
Does the hon. gentleman say that subsection 2 does not disfranchise people who, under the Naturalization Act. are British subjects?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let us keep to one difficulty at a time; the hon. gentleman has mentioned another class of people, but we are trying to deal with the particular class of people in regard to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pardee) has spoken. They are a class of people who never were naturalized. That is conceded, I understand. All this discussion is in the interest of a class of people who were not naturalized, who would desire to be naturalized but who are blocked in that respect by the ten-year requirement of the Naturalization Act.
Some of these persons were naturalized by the operation of law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Suppose that there is a class also which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cannon) is interested in, it will make for clearness if we deal with each class by itself. The obstacle that is in the way of the particular class we are concerned with is the obstacle in the way of their becoming British subjects. If they could get over the obstacle of becoming British subjects under the Naturalization Act there would he no obstacle in the way of their voting. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Pardee) wants to remedy that condition, and he suggests, as I understand, that the way to remedy that condition is to be found in this Act. It means that he wants to do it by providing that all those people who continue not to



be British subjects shall nevertheless have the vote.
Mr. PARD.EE: What I mean is that those people who have not been naturalized cannot be naturalized until ten years after the signing of the armistice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

My contention is that
this Act should provide that these people who are not alien enemies, without waiting for the period of ten years, should be entitled to become naturalized.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The contention is that
we should by this Act amend the Naturalization Act?
Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not going to suggest it cannot be done. I would like to suggest another possible alternative by which we could both meet the case of these people and at the same .time avoid the complications which would result from our amending the Naturalization Act without having come to some understanding by which that amendment could not interfere with the Imperial nature of our naturalization. If we could get at that, if we could get the remedy in that way, it would seem to me that it would be possible to meet the situation by common consent.
What is the remedy?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As the Acting Solicitor General has pointed out the subject is one of negotiation with the Home government at the present time. If one were quite certain that we were going to have an election tomorrow, or in six months, or at sometime that would cause this legislation to operate to the serious detriment of anybody, that might be an argument to be urged for not pushing further our endeavours to. conciliate the two positions. But the matter is now actually being dealt with, and actively dealt with. My hon. friend, the Acting Solicitor General, is not as sanguine as I am. Perhaps he has not the sanguine temperament of the people of my race.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Of your youth.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Very well, of my
youth; but speaking frankly I do not myself see, why we should apprehend that we must wait until the Imperial Conference in 1921 to have this matter adjusted. Speaking in all earnestness I would be anxious, and I think I can say that on behalf of the Government-the Prime Min-

ister (Sir Robert Borden) quite some time ago undertook, at all events, to bring the npatter up-to find a manner whereby, without having either to dislocate our Imperial naturalization on the one hand, or to provide that these people may vote if they are not British subjects on the other hand-which I think would not be a desirable alternative-we could get at such an adjustment of this difficulty about the Naturalization Act as would remove the obstacle that stands in the way of that class of people, as to whom at all events-those of them who have been described to us this evening-I think there would be a general agreement that they were deserving of sympathy in this matter; at all events for myself I would not hesitate to say that I think they are. After all, so far as they are concerned, all that we are doing by this Act is to adhere to the requirement that a man must be a British subject^ in order to vote. Seriously, I hardly think the House would consider it desirable- if it is possible to attain the result in any other way-to introduce the novelty into our system of saying that people who are not British subjects may be entitled to vote.
Let them be naturalized.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Then you have got to
deal with them by dealing with the question of naturalization; and I would think it is preferable to deal with that question of naturalization in connection with the Naturalization Act, and in such a manner -if that be possible-as to meet the difficulty that now arises without jeopardizing or prejudicing the effect which ought to be attached, and which is attached at present, to our naturalizations. It was only as the result of very long negotiations, and a good deal of patience and of perseverance, that we attained the result which we have attained without sacrificing the principle for which the hon. gentleman spoke so eloquently-the principle that nobody but this Parliament ought to decide'who ought to vote in Canada, or to decide who ought to be a naturalized British subject in Canada. It was only after a good deal of patience and persevering action that we arrived at the result which we have attained to-day under which the naturalization that comes from no authority in this world but the Canadian Parliament is recognized as an effective naturalization throughout the Empire. Now that is a very desirable thing, in the interest of all Canadian citizens.

May I point out to the
minister that we have to take it all or nothing; with its defects and faults we have to swallow7 it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. We took it after it had been modified in most important respects upon the representations of the Government of Canada.

Then we agreed to the
ten years' disqualification?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The ten years' disqualification did not come in simultaneously with our naturalizations becoming Imperial. There was no ten-year disqualification in the legislation of 1914; the ten-year disqualification came as a subsequent provision in 1919. Before 1919 w7e had a Naturalization Act fixing the conditions of naturalization which we agreed to. It is true they were not all of them what we originally suggested; but neither were they all of them what Great Britain originally suggested. Nevertheless we came to an agreement-and let me say in parenthesis in passing that it was one of the most effective and clear-cut recognitions of our right to determine for ourselves the question of naturalization which was one of the few questions that remained in dispute. When we started out in the negotiations it- was assumed in Great Britain that they would pass a Naturaliza ion Act and that by virtue of their Act of Parliament their naturalizations would be effective in this country, but that was not the way the legislation finally passed. Their naturalizations are effective in this country because a section of a statute of the Canadian Parliament confers the power upon the Secretary of State over there to grant certificates of naturalization which shall be effective in Canada, just as their Parliament gives to us power to grant certificates that shall be effective in that country. There is no more outstanding piece of evidence of the recognition of equality of status than that very naturalization legislation, but- that was not the way in which the matter was put forward to us at the outset. We had a year or so of negotiation. Now what have we achieved? We had achieved that situation before this legislation of 1919 that on conditions agreed upon, which made our legislation similar, our naturalizations obtained this great advantage, and their naturalizations obtained the same advantage by our legislation. Then came this desire on the part of the United Kingdom, and apparently certain 132*
other of the Dominions, to enact this exceptional provision arising out of the war. Now, of course to maintain our naturalizations Imperial it became necessary that we should keep our legislation similar or at least it was so thought; and it was, as I understand,-as to this I am not speaking from my own personal knowledge, I was absent when the legislation was passed- to meet that requirement of obtaining uniformity that the provision as to the ten years which had been adopted m Great Britain was adopted in this Parliament. My suggestion would be that we should make our best endeavour to obtain a remedy for that without disrupting our Imperial naturalizations, before we resort to what the hon. gentleman points out it is perfectly possible for us to do-repeal the provision which makes our naturalization similar to that of the United Kingdom, and I believe with that of the other dominions; I think they have all passed it, at all events whether that be so or not, to make it similar to that of the United Kingdom. Before we resqrt to that, before we say. " We have this thing that we want to remedy and we will pitch our Imperial naturalization to the winds for the sake of remedying that." Perhaps it would be justifiable to do so, I am not going to discuss that question now. Perhaps the remedy of this thing is worth that but I do not think we have reached that stage yet-let us make, at all events, our best endeavour to see if we cannot find a proper remedy for this difficulty without jeopardizing or without sacrificing the Imperial nature of our naturalization. I am hopeful that we shall find an adjustment of this difficulty which will enable us to preserve the Imperial nature of our naturalization and at the same time to meet the deserving cases that have been pointed out. I do not know that it is necessary for us this evening to consider whether this ten-year clause might not be properly applicable to some class of people. I do not know whether it would be suggested, for instance, that as regards people coming in in the future

The Minister intimates that he is hopeful of an adjustment. May I suggest that those who are being debarred from the right to vote under the Act by reason of the provisions of the Naturalization Act be placed in the same position as women are now placed in who become British subjects by operation of law, namely, the position under which, they may, if they have resided five years in Canada prior to the passing of the Naturalization

Act, 1919, go before a judge, take the oath of allegiance, and, provided they are otherwise properly qualified, be granted the right to vote? Why should those whom it is now proposed to debar be placed in a worse position than the women?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The women we are including are women who are British subjects and who, if they had not become British subjects by their marriage, for instance, would on their own qualifications have been entitled to become British subjects.
So would these men.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The difficulty with' these men is that they are not British subjects, and under the existing Naturalization Law cannot become British subjects; and if this Act is going to give them the right to vote it will have to do so notwithstanding that they are not British subjects. On the other hand, the women my hon. friend speaks of are British subjects by marriage, and without this legislation would have the right to vote.
They are British subjects, but they cannot vote unless they get this certificate.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is a different question.
It is not a different question so far as the purposes of this Act are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They are a class of people from whom the vote to which they would otherwise be entitled is taken by this Act.
And from the wives and the children.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If this Act had not stepped in, these women, having become British subjects by marriage, or the children, having become British subjects by the naturalization of their fathers, would have had a .vote. This Act steps in and says that people naturalized in that way, though they are British subjects,-it -does not say they are not British subjects-
But it is the question of giving them the vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This Act takes the vote from them.
But it gives it back to them if they get this certificate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Subject to certain conditions, it gives it back, but in doing both [Mr Pardee.]
these things it is dealing with the right to vote,-granting or refusing, but always granting or refusing to a person who is a British subject. But as to the other class, we have to get over that other hurdle; perhaps it is only a sentimental thing-

I think it is.
Mr. DOHERTY-: But I am not so sure that there are not some sentimental things that have value in the life of a nation.
Quite true.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Surely the hon. gentleman will concede that it would be an undesirable thing to give the vote to a man who is not a British subject; that it would be better to find a way to make him a British subject than to try to find a way to give him a vote when he is not a British subject.
If you take the vote away from a British subject you may as well give it to one wdio is not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are other British subjects who do not have votes.

The minister's chief argument as against giving the vote to the first class, those who are not British subjects, was that that would involve an amendment of the Naturalization Law, and, as regards the second class, the wives and children, the electoral law says that they must secure from a judge a certificate before voting. According to the Naturalization Act, these people are British subjects. Section 1, paragraph 3 of the Naturalization Act says:
Nothing in this section shall, except as otherwise expressly provided, affect the status of any person born before the commencement of this Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That applies only to
natural-born British subjects.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Read the heading.

I have read it. So that
according to this Act a woman is a British subject and her status can be changed by the Franchise Act. If we change it as is done in the Franchise Act, we are amending the Naturalization Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I shall be glad, so far
as it is in my power to do so, to throw any light I can upon the questions arising in regard to the women and the children under this section. But, as I said before, I would like to keep clearly distinct the two classes with which we have been dealing.

In that regard, it does seem to me that our best method is to exhaust every means of meeting the difficulty that results from the Naturalization Act, treating it as a naturalization question, before we resort to amendments to an election Act for the - purpose of removing that difficulty-amendments that may cost us the very high price of loss of our Imperial naturalization or of putting upon us in the alternative of taking the position that though we cannot make these people British subjects, yet we give them the vote. This does not seem to me to be the proper origin of the grievance- The grievance is born not of this Act, but of the Naturalization Act. This Act itself, so far as these people are concerned, continues to recognize the principle that the right to vote applies to the British subject or citizen; that that is a sine qua non to the right to vote. All British subjects have not the right to vote, but up to the present no man who is not a British subject has had the right to vote. Now, it is a serious thing to suggest departing from that, and I think that hon. gentlemen might be satisfied to give us an opportunity to see whether we can meet the difficulty in dealing with the Naturalization Act, and to allow this Bill, which upon this question only stands by the principle that to be a voter you must be a 'British subject, to pass, so far as this particular provision is concerned.

I should like to make a
few observations and to suggest what appears to me to be a very reasonable and . logical remedy. At the outset I may repeat that it should be perfectly plain to the members of the Committee that there are two groups of people under discussion, and that the amendment itself only applies to those who are British subjects by operation of law.
I believe the amedment will give them the franchise if they fulfil a certain condition. But we have entered to-night upon a discussion of another matter, the status of another group of people in this country, who are not Canadian citizens because they are not naturalized, but to whom naturalization should be given. I think the Government itself is admitting that this second group of people, smaller than the first, is of a kind worthy of naturalization because they have for many years considered themselves British subjects. I admit that, in order that this second group of people may be permitted to vote, they must first obtain naturalization, and that the remedy must come through an amendment to the Naturalization Act or the
enactment of a new law that will give them the franchise.
When the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) states that it is desirable that all Canadian citizens naturalized in future shall have Imperial naturalization, I agree with him entirely, and I believe that is a highly desirable thing. Last year when the new Naturalization Act was under consideration and the status of these people' was being discussed, the Prime Minister at that time promised to take the matter up with the Imperial Government in order that a modification might be made that would permit of the naturalization of these alien people. The Minister of Justice to-night states that he is quite optimistic that that modification will be made. I am very glad to hear that; but I am just a little dubious about the rapidity with which that may be obtained, in the light of what has already taken place, or rather has not so far taken place, because the Naturalization Act of 1919 was passed almost a year ago and it is almost a year since the promise was made, quite honestly and sincerely I think, by the Prime Minister that he *yvould attempt to obtain that modification; yet, to-day, so far as we know, we are precisely in the same position as regards these people as we were a year ago. I fear that if progress is not any more rapid than it has been, it may quite well come to the time of another election before justice is rendered to these people. It was not, apparently, the intention of the British Government, nor of the representatives of the Dominion when this matter was discussed at the Peace Conference, that the Dominions should be tied hard and fast to that ten-year clause. I think the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) will bear me out in that regard, because I think either he himself or the Prime Minister said on the floor of this House last year, when the Naturalization Act was under discussion, that it was intended and stated than that it should be possible for the Dominions, Such as Canada, where conditions differed from those in England, to vary their laws with regard to people such as those whose case we have been discussing to-night. I think I am right in that. Yet when the Act was. put through the British Parliament, it was so framed, inadvertently, that it became necessary for the Dominions to adopt that holus-bolus as their own. If it be true that it was not originally the intention to make the Act so stringent in this country, and if this slipped, if I may use that expression, inadvertently-into the British Act so that it became neces-

sary to make ours the same in order to conform with it, then it should not be difficult to obtain the consent of the British authorities to such a modification, and to obtain it very quickly if it was not originally the intention that the Act should be framed as it is at present. I throw that out as a suggestion. I mean to convey the idea that it should be possible to obtain from the British Government a consent to the modification very quickly, if possible, before this House rises. I should like to make the further suggestion, that if the Government receives a negative reply from the British Government, it then surely becomes the-duty of the Canadian Parliament to protect its people by giving them Canadian naturalization.
I want to make this suggestion also, which I think is fair and would solve the difficulty with regard to this group of people which I am free to admit is, not as large as the other group which is being enfranchised under this amendment. Why could not this Parliament simply enact, for the purpose of these people, the old naturalization law giving them only Canadian citizenship? I do not mean to say that we should keep on our statute books two naturalization laws permanently; but in order to meet the fair demands of these people who have waited a long time, why should we not re-enact the law which would give them Canadian naturalization, and then, just so soon as you obtain a modification of the Act of last year, we can repeal the Canadian naturalization law? I do not see why that suggestion could not be accepted, and if it could, it would solve the difficulty.
While I am on my feet I should like again to make the suggestion that I do not see what possible harm could be done- and this would obviate the difficulty with regard to these British subjects who are British subjects by operation of law-if you simply strike out subclause 2 of clause 29 and base the vote on broad British citizenship instead of compelling women-and this is absolutely true as I showed the other night-who have had sons at the war, who have had sons killed in the war- to appear before a judse in order to prove that they are worthy of the franchise, when it is admitted that they are British subjects, and when their husbands can go to the polls without appearing before a judge. They are British subjects by operation of the law, so why should they have to appear before a judge to prove that they have a light to vote?

I sympathize very warmly with the view of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) that we should, if possible, find a remedy for this grievance without interfering with the Naturalization Act which is, I think, of great value and importance to Canada. We had, as has been referred to in this discussion, a number of very distinguished citizens in Canada who thought they were British subjects, but who, while they were British subjects on this side of the Atlantic, discovered that they were not British subjects when they landed in Great Britain. After many years an Imperial Naturalization Act was enacted. The distinguished gentleman who is High Commissioner for Canada in London at the present time discovered when he got over there that he was not' a British subject although he was a minister of the Crown in Canada. He was born in the United States; he was naturalized in Canada; he was a British subject for all our purposes, but he was not a British subject in Great. Britain. It was to remedy that case and other cases of a like character that the Imperial Naturalization Act was passed. I think, in the main, that law is a good one. The Minister of Justice and the Acting Solicitor General have repeatedly referred to negotiations that have been in progress with respect to the naturalization law. I wonder if my hon friends could tell me what was the Objective of which the Minister of Justice is so hopeful but of which the Acting Solicitor General is not so hopeful.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The difference in our hopefulness is only as to period of time and not as to ultimate attainment. What we had in mind was to endeavour to have an agreement whereby this particular provision of ten years should not be insisted upon as being essential of application in all of the Dominions concerned in order that the certificate of that Dominion should be accepted as meeting the essential requirements for Imperial naturalization. Speaking for myself it seems to me it ought to be possible that, while yo.u might insist upon certain fundamental things as being essential to the legislation of all the countries concerned, in order that the naturalization be effective throughout all those countries, there might fairly be left a certain play of discretion for each country to make additional requirements which it considers necessary to meet its own peculiar conditions.

Who will make the
decision as to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The decision, like all
other decisions where you are trying to get concurrent action, would have to be by agreement.

A conference?
Air. DOHERTY": You may do something by correspondence, you may do something by getting together, but I would hope that such a decision might be arrived at without calling a formal Imperial Conference to discuss the matter. I cannot promise, I do not know how it will strike other people. The hon. gentleman asked what wTas the purpose we had in view. The purpose we had in view, having this particular thing in mind, but not confining ourselves absolutely to that, was, speaking for myself, just what I have stated, that it ought to be possible. We have laid the foundation, we have got all these essential conditions which everybody was agreed should be the conditions of imperial naturalization, and it seems to me it ought to be quite within the bounds of possibility to continue to recognize all round the naturalizations as imperial as long as those fundamental things are adhered to, but still leave some opportunity for making suitable provisions in each country to meet conditions that may be peculiar to itself, those conditions taking the form of additional requirements.

The ten-year clause, I understand, is the real cause of the trouble; that is the snag. I understand that what *my hon. friend has in mind is that they shall induce the British Government and the other parties to agree to reduce that period either generally or as respects Canada. Am I right?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is the object.

I understand that the hon. gentleman suggests that it might be reduced. Well, I know enough about the slowness of making changes over there to be a little less confident than my hon. friend is as to an early solution along these lines. The desire for uniformity in a naturalization law is very strong, and a proposal that you vary that Uniformity and provide that there may be one condition for one Dominion and another condition for another will be objected to very strongly. I am inclined to think that the British Government will be slow to agree to a change. If I could feel it was coming very quickly, perhaps I would not feel there *was any need of doing anything else. But why should we not in the meantime act
on the suggestion of my hon. friend from North Waterloo and provide that these people who should be qualified, being naturalized under our hitherto law, so to speak, shall continue to be deemed British subjects in Canada for the purpose of voting. My hon. friend (Mr. Doherty) has said they are not British subjects. He assumes that now we have adopted this naturalization law a man can only be a British subject when he is a British subject recognized by the Imperial Act. But we have had two kinds of naturalization law in Canada for fifty years. We have had a naturalization law for Great Britain, and we have had a naturalization law for Canada. I agree that it' is desirable that there should be uniformity, but we have had two kinds of naturalization law for half a century, and when we find that by this sudden change we are shutting out a worthy class of our people ' from the privilege of the franchise I can see no difficulty in passing .an Act not touching naturalization law for imperial purposes, but providing that these persons, being otherwise properly qualified, shall be deemed to be British subjects in Canada so far as to entitle them to vote. I see no difficulty in doing that at all.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Aly hon. friend is in error in his statement that we have had two classes of naturalization under ^ our Canadian law for the past fifty years. Speaking from recollection, we only had the one Act relating to. naturalization in force prior to the recent imperial naturalization going into effect.

My hon. friend sees
what I mean.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is quite true that a man born a British subject had the rights of a British citizen in all portions of the Empire. In that Tespect he stood in a different position from the man naturalized under our Canadian law, who did not have the right of British citizenship outside the Dominion.
As my hon. friend from North Waterloo has referred to the proceedings of the Imperial Conference when these and kindred questions were under consideration I desire to make just a brief reference to that, because I think it will throw some light on the present situation and on the prospect of reaching an understanding with the British .government in reference to it. There are in the Imperial Naturalization Law-I am now referring to the Act passed by the British House of Commons in 1919 amend-
Does the minister think that it is within the bounds of probability, at any rate, that we may get that reply from the British Government before the House rises?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is possible; I cannot say that it is probable.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Would it not be possible to take up this matter by cable through the High Commissioner in London at once with a view to obtaining some answer that could be given to Parliament in a day or two?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I doubt whether we could get an answer in a day or two. My hon. friend will realize that in connection with

i
matters of this kind you are not likely to get a reply in such a brief space of time. I may say, however, that it is the intention of the Minister of Justice to use the cable, and so far as lies within our power, we shall secure the earliest possible reply.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am glad to hear the minister say that it is the intention of the Government to take this matter up by cable. I should think that if the Government were to represent to the British authorities that this Parliament is in session and is anxious to have this matter settled before prorogation, there would be every tendency on the part of the British office to facilitate matters. It is just a matter of the Government making their representations strong enough.
Will it be possible for the House to, amend the Naturalization Act before the British Parliament has amended its Act in this particular?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
1 think the Act would
have to be amended by the British Parliament before our naturalization could be made effective. All we could get by cable would be the answer of the British Government that they would or would not submit legislation to Parliament to cover the matter; but I should think that if they submitted legislation to Parliament that legislation would go- through.
Mr. 'EULER: But it would not be possible for this Parliament to enact legislation at this session, under the best circumstances, according to the statement of the minister. If before we can legally do anything in this matter it is necessary for the British Parliament first to make their change, then, if they are not now in session, it would be impossible for us to enact legislation at this session.
iMr. ROWELL: One cannot, of course, say anything so far as that is concerned until one knows what answer the British Government will make as to what they are prepared to do.

I would not
presume to follow the more or less involved legal discussion that has taken place tonight; but it seems to me, if I have been able to grasp the trend of the debate, that it is in the mind of the Government and of those who have been discussing this subject that the enactment of 1919, under which enemy aliens of German, Austrian, Bulgarian or Turkish origin cannot be granted the franchise in Canada or be naturalized
for ten years after the signing of the Armistice, is to be amended and we are going to go back to conditions that prevailed before 1914 under which all these classes, without any effort being made to determine their qualifications for Canadian citizenship, might be naturalized and, as I heard an hon. member say tonight, be made Canadian citizens by the hundred overnight. I realize that what my hon. friend from North Waterloo has said with regard to certain individuals who have lived in this country for a long time may be correct; there may be some people of that class. But I would say to my hon. friend in this connection that- if, as I understood him and as I think I understood the hon. member for West Lambton to say, there are men who have lived in Canada fer twenty, thirty or forty years, having come to this country from Germany, Austria or Bulgaria, and who had not become British subjects up to 1914, then, having lived in Canada all these years prior to 1914 without having manifested any desire to become British or Canadian citizens willing to share the full responsibilities which Canadians had to bear during the years of the war, they can very well wait for the period of time which it has been deemed wise for men of enemy countries to wait following the signing of the Armistice.

(Is the 'hon. member aware that some of the men of whom he speaks actually had sons in the war who cannot get naturalization now?
.'Mr. NICHOLSON: I appreciate that fact, and if a means can be found to remedy that condition without opening the door wide, as is the apparent desire to-night, to all of these people of enemy origin so as to allow them to become enfranchised citizens, then I would be willing to go all the way in the interests of those men who had seen service in the war. But the whole trend of the discussion has implied a desire on the part of hon. members, not to rectify such specific defects as mentioned by my hon. friend (Mr. Euler), but to go back to conditions under which we were having dumped into sections of this country, night and day through a slipshod form of enfranchisement, hundreds of people who knew absolutely nothing of Canadian ideals and who evidenced the fact that they lacked all sense of Canadianism; for if they had Canadian ideals they would have become Canadian citizens before 1914. I am not considering this question from any partisan

standpoint, but I say that it is absolutely unfair to those Canadian citizens who bore the burden of the war to say, now that the war is over, that we are going to open the door wide to Germans, Austrians, Bulgarians and Turks, and tell those people: "You can come to Canada and get identically the same privileges as are enjoyed by those citizens who palyed their part in the war and whose sons stood face to face with men of your origin in the trenches in France and Flanders and elsewhere". Before the Government goes very far in the direction of throwing the door wide open let me warn them that they are going to raise a question in this country that will not be easily settled.

I would like to call the attention of . the Government to the difficulty of getting an answer from the British Government. Before an answer can be given it will require a decision of the British Government and decisions of governments, even of this Government, are not obtained very quickly. Having obtained the' decision of the British Government, you require to have an Act of the British Parliament and that is something that will be attended with much difficulty. The minister has told us that negotiations were conducted between the British and Canadian Governments before this Act was framed. I take it that there were similar negotiations with the governments of the other British dominions. This Act has been something in the nature of a Treaty between Canada, Great Britain and the various overseas dominions and they will all have to be consulted before a change takes place. Taking all these things into account I am not in the least bit sanguine that a measure of immediate relief can be obtained in that direction. If there is a grievance, and the minister thinks there is a grievance, I think it will be better to seek the remedy in another way.

This section requires a few amendments in order to be acceptable. I think the Gordian knot ought to be cut by the minister who has (the Bill in charge by striking out subsection 2 completely. That would give satisfaction all round. I consider subsection 2 a blot upon the Bill. To my mind it is nothing but arrant nonsense. I have stated this several times before when Franchise Bills similar to this were before the House, and I see nothing so far to cause me to change my view. We have not heard a word this evening in justification of the second part of subsection 2 which makes a distinction between fMr. Nicholson.]
people born on the continent of North America and people bom in other parts of the world. The minister has not so far enlightened us as to why this distinction is being made. Before proceeding any further I should like to know why it is found in this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Because we recognize that people born on this continent are very similar in their ideas, laws, customs and habits to our own people and we can very quickly assimilate them to our ways, and that therefore we permit them to vote without any injustice to ourselves and without as long a period of probation as we require of people from central Europe or from other parts of the world.
Not central Europe. This takes in the whole of Europe, and includes France and Belgium.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: From Europe. They are not accustomed to our ways, language, laws and political institutions. That is the reason for the distinction to be found in the Bill. Perhaps there may be other reasons, but that is the main reason. I think I can assure the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) that the Government has no intention whatever of indiscriminately opening wide the door to permit all the classes of people that we have been discussing to-night to come in and obtain naturalization as British subjects. There will be investigation and inquiry. There may be some worthy and some unworthy ones and I do not for a moment say that all the fathers of the boys who served in the war should vote. Certainly they will never vote in my riding with my consent. I could cite the concrete case of two young men of German parentage who went to the war, one of whom won the military cross. The father would not allow them to come home to bid good-bye to their mother; he threatened to shoot them. Do you think that man should have a vote? I would keep that man ten years on probation. I do not say that is the general thing but I do say that no government would be justified in indiscriminately throwing open the door and admitting everybody. There would be an inquiry so that the worthy ones may be rewarded and the unworthy ones put on probation.
The swallow-tail-coat Act.

Yes, the swallow-tail-coat Act as my hon. friend has said. But the trouble, Mr. Chairman, is that we always like to worship something from afar; we like to worship false gods; and we find ourselves in this condition purely because we dropped and wiped off the statute books

an Act that would have given satisfaction all around, and took on this legislation which gives satisfaction to none. I do not know how the Government are going to explain to any respectable body of foreign-born what they had in mind by putting on the statute books this subsection 2 of section 29. The hon. gentleman thinks he has improved it with amendments. I remember when the weakness in the armour was discovered by the hon. member for'North Waterloo on the occasion of the second reading o'f the Bill. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) rushed to -the rescue and pointed out that the section did not mean what it said it meant. Now the Acting Solicitor General has introduced an amendment which he says, in effect, is going to correct the difficulty. The hon. member for North Waterloo, however, says that the Under Secretary of State agrees with him and disagrees with the Acting Solicitor General with regard to the meaning of certain words in this section when these are read wdth the words of another section of the Act. Now all this difficulty wre can rid ourselves of toy simply striking out the section which pleases no one, and which cannot please the Acting Solicitor General -to my mind it does not, because he is too good a lawyer to believe that any section such as that would meet with any commendation from lawyers or the community generally. It is bad in its inception, it is unjust in its conception; and for that reason I could have hoped that it had been stifled in its birth. I am satisfied to accept the other sections of the Bill, which I read over very carefully, and which I think are fairly just.	-
Not all.

Not all, but as much as we could expect from gentlemen who do not think as we do in some things. I scarcely believe the phrase, "nothing good can come out of Nazareth." Sometimes something good does come out; and I would be willing to give my unqualified praise if the hon. gentleman will consent, now that he is in an amending mood, to strike out this obnoxious clause from the Act. I may say that so long as I am a member of the House -this is not in the way of a threat, but it is a prediction-I will introduce, year after year, Bills to amend this obnoxious section, if it becomes law, until it is finally taken from the statute book. In other words I intend to picket the Government-I trust the Minister of Justice undertsands what I

mean toy that-I intend to picket the Government until this obnoxious section is removed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the amendment
carry?

No. This important
amendment has not been half discussed yet, we are only getting started. I move that the committee rise and report progress. It is one o'clock. The Railway Committee meets in a few hours, and there are important measures to be brought before that committee. I think we have done a good day's work. Sitting from three o'clock in the afternoon till one o'clock the next morning is a longer spell than my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council, at the International Labour Conference, agreed to allow the people to work in this country, and we do not want to set a bad example.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
We have not done very badly to-night, we have done fairly well, and were we to sit for another hour we would have done even better. I have no objection under the circumstances to ask the committee to rise and report progress.
Progress reported. _
On the motion of Rt. Hon. Mr. Doherty, the House adjourned at 1.05' a.m. (Thursday) .
